title: ISO 27001, SOC 2 & Compliance Assurance — VVnT SeQuor
content:
Terminology
The words we use — and what they mean .
Precise language matters in assurance. This is how we use these terms across our site, proposals and reports.
Assessment An evaluation of a system, product or organization against defined criteria (for example a gap assessment, VAPT or accessibility conformance assessment). It produces findings, not a certificate.

title: ISO 27001, SOC 2 & Compliance Assurance — VVnT SeQuor
content:
Audit A systematic, independent and documented examination against an audit standard or criteria — for example an internal audit of your ISMS performed by VVnT SeQuor.
Readiness Preparing your organization for an external certification audit or attestation. We implement and prepare; we do not certify.
Certification Formal certification against a scheme such as ISO/IEC 27001, issued only by an independent, accredited certification body. VVnT SeQuor is not a certification body.

title: ISO 27001, SOC 2 & Compliance Assurance — VVnT SeQuor
content:
Attestation An independent report such as SOC 2, issued by a licensed CPA firm. We prepare you for it.
Assurance certificate A VVnT POC Assurance Certificate — POC stands for Proof of Compliance — is a VVnT-issued artifact recording the scope, criteria, evidence and outcome of our independent assessment of an AI deployment or product (via VVnT Accreditation). It is not an ISO certification or an accreditation.

title: ISO 27001, SOC 2 & Compliance Assurance — VVnT SeQuor
content:
Accreditation In conformity-assessment, accreditation is granted to certification bodies and labs by national accreditation bodies. “VVnT Accreditation” is our product name for AI assurance and is not an accreditation-body designation.
Conformance report A statement of how a product conforms to a standard such as WCAG — e.g. an Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR) on the VPAT® template. A VPAT is a reporting format, not a certification.

What is VVnT Accreditation?
VVnT Accreditation is VVnT SeQuor's independent AI and product assurance service. title: How Security, ISO & AI Assurance Connect — VVnT SeQuor
content:
What does POC stand for in the VVnT POC Assurance Certificate?
POC stands for Proof of Compliance. It's a VVnT-issued assurance artifact recording the scope, criteria, evidence and outcome of an independent review — not an ISO/IEC management-system certification or an accreditation under any national accreditation scheme. See the full terminology →
Is the relationship between Assure & Comply and Build & Engineer one-way or two-way?

title: How Security, ISO & AI Assurance Connect — VVnT SeQuor
content:
It's continuous and two-way. Assure & Comply practices — security, ISO compliance, privacy, accessibility — define what "good" looks like for Build & Engineer practices to build against, and AI testing and build-stage findings feed back to refine that bar. This mirrors how NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001 both frame AI governance as an ongoing loop rather than a one-time handoff — see how the two frameworks compare →
How many ways can an engagement with VVnT SeQuor start?

title: How Security, ISO & AI Assurance Connect — VVnT SeQuor
content:
How many ways can an engagement with VVnT SeQuor start?
Four common triggers, and any one of them works as an entry point: a customer audit, an investor review, a procurement checklist, or a certification deadline. Each maps into whichever Assure & Comply practices apply, so there's no single required starting point.
Does VVnT Accreditation issue ISO certifications or accreditation-body designations?

title: How Security, ISO & AI Assurance Connect — VVnT SeQuor
content:
No. VVnT Accreditation is VVnT SeQuor's own independent assurance service, not an accreditation body recognized under a national accreditation scheme. For ISO/IEC management-system certification itself, VVnT SeQuor prepares clients for audits performed by accredited, independent certification bodies. Explore ISO & Compliance Implementation →
Who governs VVnT Accreditation's review standards?

title: How Security, ISO & AI Assurance Connect — VVnT SeQuor
content:
Who governs VVnT Accreditation's review standards?
VVNT Foundation designs the standards, practices and SOPs that VVnT Accreditation reviews against. VVnT SeQuor delivers the engagement being reviewed. Keeping these separate — who sets the bar, who is reviewed, and who reviews independently — follows the same structural separation the IIA's Three Lines Model uses for governance internationally.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Knowledge Hub · Glossary
One definition for every term, linked from everywhere.
Terms across every practice — defined once in plain language, with a worked example for almost every one. Pick a practice below to see just its terms, or search across all of them.
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , Founder & CTO, VVnT SeQuor · Last reviewed October 2026

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
All terms (262) Cybersecurity & Cyber Assurance (45) ISO & Compliance Implementation (42) Privacy & Data Protection (37) Accessibility & Inclusive Product Engineering (31) GenAI & Agentic AI Development (31) AI Testing & Evaluations (26) Digital Testing & Automation (25) Strategic IT & Architecture Advisory (25)
Cybersecurity & Cyber Assurance
Go deeper: Cybersecurity overview · Pre-VAPT Readiness & Scoping Checklist

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Go deeper: Cybersecurity overview · Pre-VAPT Readiness & Scoping Checklist
VAPT (Vulnerability Assessment & Penetration Testing) A combined exercise that first scans systems for known vulnerabilities (the assessment) and then actively attempts to exploit them under controlled conditions (the penetration test), producing a prioritized, evidence-backed list of exploitable weaknesses rather than just a raw scan report.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example A fintech runs an annual VAPT before its SOC 2 audit — the pen test report becomes direct evidence for the audit.
Penetration Testing An authorized, simulated attack against a system, network or application to find exploitable weaknesses before a real attacker does. Scope, rules of engagement and timing are agreed in advance with the organization being tested.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example A web app pen test reveals that a password-reset link never expires, letting an attacker take over any account found in an old data leak.
Zero Trust Architecture A security model that removes implicit trust from network location: every user, device and service must be authenticated and authorized for each request, not just once at the network perimeter. Increasingly applied to non-human identities — service accounts and AI agents — as well as people.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example An employee's laptop is re-verified before every internal app it connects to, not just once when it joins the office Wi-Fi.
Non-Human Identity A service account, API key, workload identity or AI agent that authenticates and acts within a system without a person directly at the keyboard. Non-human identities now outnumber human ones in most enterprises and need their own lifecycle, least-privilege and monitoring controls.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example A CI/CD pipeline's service account that deploys code to production is a non-human identity — and a prime target if it carries admin rights everywhere.
Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) Continuous, automated checking of cloud environments against security best practices and benchmarks, to catch misconfigurations — an overly permissive storage bucket, an open security group — before they become breaches, especially across multi-cloud estates.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example A CSPM tool flags a storage bucket set to public-read within minutes, instead of the misconfiguration being found during next year's audit.
Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM) A cyclical programme — scoping, discovery, prioritization, validation and mobilization — for continuously finding and reducing an organization's exploitable attack surface, replacing point-in-time vulnerability scans with an ongoing process.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example Instead of one annual VAPT, a CTEM programme runs continuous discovery and validation, re-prioritizing exposures as the environment changes week to week.
Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Cryptographic algorithms designed to remain secure against attacks from future quantum computers. Relevant today because of “harvest now, decrypt later” — encrypted data intercepted now could be stored and decrypted once quantum computing matures.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example A bank migrates its VPN to PQC-ready algorithms today, even though large-scale quantum computers don't exist yet, to protect data that must stay confidential for decades.
Vulnerability A weakness in a system, application or process that could be exploited to cause harm — distinct from a threat (the potential cause of harm) and risk (the likelihood and impact if a threat actually exploits that vulnerability).

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example An unpatched web server running an outdated library version is a vulnerability, whether or not anyone has tried to exploit it yet.
Threat Anything with the potential to exploit a vulnerability and cause harm — an attacker, a piece of malware, a natural disaster, or even a careless insider.
Example A disgruntled former employee who still has valid credentials is a threat, independent of whether a system vulnerability exists for them to exploit.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Exploit A piece of code, technique or sequence of commands that takes advantage of a specific vulnerability to cause unintended behavior, such as gaining unauthorized access.
Example A proof-of-concept script that takes advantage of an unpatched SQL injection flaw to extract a database's contents is an exploit.
Malware Malicious software designed to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorized access to a system — an umbrella term covering viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware and spyware.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example A free "PDF converter" download that secretly installs a keylogger is malware, regardless of which specific category it falls into.
Ransomware Malware that encrypts a victim's data and demands payment for the decryption key, often combined with a threat to leak the stolen data if payment isn't made.
Example The 2021 Colonial Pipeline attack, where ransomware shut down fuel distribution across the US East Coast, remains a widely cited case study.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Phishing A social engineering attack that uses deceptive emails, messages or websites to trick someone into revealing credentials or payment details, or into installing malware.
Example An email impersonating IT, asking an employee to "verify their password" via a fake login page, is a classic phishing attempt.
Social Engineering Manipulating people, rather than systems, into breaking normal security procedure — impersonation, pretexting, urgency and appeals to authority are common tactics.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example A caller impersonating the help desk, pressuring an employee to reset an executive's MFA device "right now," is social engineering — no malware involved at all.
Firewall A network security device or software that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing traffic based on defined rules, forming a basic perimeter defense.
Example A firewall rule blocking all inbound traffic on port 3389 (RDP) from the public internet closes off a commonly exploited attack path.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Encryption Converting data into a coded form that can only be read with the correct key, protecting it whether it's stored (at rest) or being transmitted (in transit).
Example HTTPS encrypts data in transit between a browser and a website; full-disk encryption protects a stolen laptop's data at rest.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) Requiring two or more independent proofs of identity to log in — typically something you know (a password), something you have (a device or token), or something you are (biometrics) — so a stolen password alone can't grant access.
Example Logging in with a password plus a one-time code from an authenticator app is MFA — a stolen password alone no longer gets an attacker in.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Least Privilege The principle of giving a user, service or system only the minimum access needed to do its job, limiting the damage if that account is ever compromised.
Example A marketing analyst's account can read the sales dashboard but can't modify production database records — access matched to the job, not the org chart.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Attack Surface The complete set of points — systems, APIs, accounts, physical devices — where an attacker could potentially try to gain access to or extract data from an environment.
Example Every forgotten staging server still reachable from the internet, every unused API endpoint, and every employee with email access all add to the attack surface.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Incident Response The structured process an organization follows when a security incident occurs — detect, contain, eradicate, recover and learn — to limit damage and prevent recurrence.
Example When ransomware is detected, a documented IR plan tells the team to isolate affected machines first, then notify leadership and legal, before anyone touches backups.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
SOC (Security Operations Center) A team, in-house or outsourced, that continuously monitors, detects and responds to security threats across an organization's environment.
Example A SOC analyst notices unusual login activity from an unfamiliar country at 3am and escalates it before the attacker can move further.
SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) A platform that aggregates and correlates log and event data from across an environment to detect suspicious activity in near-real time.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example A SIEM correlates a failed-login spike on one server with an unusual outbound data transfer from another, surfacing a pattern no single log would show alone.
EDR / XDR (Endpoint / Extended Detection & Response) Tools that continuously monitor endpoints — and, with XDR, email, network and cloud too — for malicious activity and enable rapid investigation and response.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example EDR on an employee's laptop detects and automatically kills a malicious process within seconds of it trying to contact a command-and-control server.
DDoS (Distributed Denial-of-Service) An attack that floods a system or network with traffic from many sources at once, overwhelming it so legitimate users can't get through.
Example An e-commerce site going down during a flash sale because of a flood of junk traffic from thousands of compromised devices is a DDoS attack.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
CVE & CVSS A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) is a unique public identifier for a known vulnerability; CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) is the standard scale, 0–10, used to rate how severe it is.
Example "CVE-2021-44228" (Log4Shell) carried a CVSS score of 10.0 — the maximum — reflecting how easily it could be exploited and how much damage it could do.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Patch Management The process of identifying, testing and deploying software updates that fix known vulnerabilities, ideally before attackers can exploit them.
Example A documented patch-management process ensures critical vulnerabilities are patched within days, not whenever someone next reboots the server.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Vulnerability Scanning Automated scanning of systems against a database of known vulnerabilities to produce a list of weaknesses — the "assessment" half of VAPT, without the active exploitation attempt a penetration test adds.
Example A weekly automated scan flags that twelve servers are still running an outdated OpenSSL version with a known vulnerability.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Bug Bounty A program that pays independent security researchers for responsibly disclosing vulnerabilities they find in an organization's systems, extending testing coverage beyond an internal team.
Example A researcher reports a flaw that lets one user view another user's private data, and is paid a bounty instead of selling it elsewhere.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
IAM (Identity and Access Management) The policies, processes and tools an organization uses to ensure the right people and systems have the right access to the right resources, and nothing more.
Example An IAM system automatically revokes a contractor's access to every connected system the moment their contract end-date passes.
Network Segmentation Dividing a network into smaller, isolated zones so that a breach in one segment can't automatically spread to the rest of the environment.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example Point-of-sale systems are kept on a separate network segment from the general office network, so a phishing-compromised laptop can't reach payment card data.
Red Team / Blue Team / Purple Team A red team simulates real attackers; a blue team defends and responds; a purple team works both sides together to turn offensive findings into better defenses faster.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Example A red team simulates a phishing-based breach; the blue team's detection is measured; a purple-team debrief turns the gaps into new SIEM alert rules.
Zero-Day Vulnerability A vulnerability that is actively being exploited, or publicly known, before the vendor has released a fix — leaving defenders with "zero days" of advance warning.
Example Attackers exploiting a browser flaw before the vendor even knows it exists leaves defenders with no patch to apply.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Supply Chain Attack An attack that compromises an organization indirectly, through a trusted third-party vendor, open-source library or software update mechanism, rather than attacking it head-on.
Example The 2020 SolarWinds breach, where attackers compromised a trusted software update to reach thousands of the vendor's customers at once, is the textbook case.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Threat Intelligence Curated, contextualized information about current and emerging threats — attacker techniques, indicators of compromise, active campaigns — used to inform defensive priorities.
Example A threat intelligence feed flags that a specific ransomware group is actively targeting the user's industry this month, prompting extra vigilance.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
CIA Triad The three core goals every security control serves: Confidentiality (only authorized people can read data), Integrity (data can't be tampered with undetected), and Availability (systems stay accessible when needed).
Example A ransomware attack is primarily an availability failure — the data may still be confidential and unaltered, but no one can access it.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Defense in Depth Layering multiple, independent security controls — network, endpoint, identity, application — so that if one layer fails, others still stand between an attacker and the target.
Example A phishing email that slips past email filtering still has to beat MFA and endpoint detection before it does real damage.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation & Response) Software that connects an organization's security tools together and automates the routine steps of investigating and responding to alerts, so analysts spend their time on judgment calls, not repetitive triage.
Example A SOAR playbook automatically isolates an infected laptop from the network the moment EDR flags it, before a human analyst opens the ticket.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Honeypot A decoy system deliberately exposed to attract attackers, giving defenders early warning of an intrusion attempt and insight into attacker techniques without risking real assets.
Example A fake, unprotected-looking database server sits on the network purely to alert the SOC the instant anyone touches it — no legitimate user ever should.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Sandboxing Running untrusted code — a suspicious email attachment, an unverified application — in an isolated environment where it can't affect the real system, to observe what it does safely.
Example An email security gateway detonates every attachment in a sandbox first; if it contacts a known malicious server, the real email never reaches the inbox.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Insider Threat Risk that originates from someone who already has legitimate access — an employee, contractor or partner — whether through malicious intent, carelessness, or a compromised account.
Example An employee emailing a customer database to their personal account the week before resigning to join a competitor is an insider threat.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Credential Stuffing An attack that automatically tries username/password pairs leaked from one breach against many other sites, exploiting the fact that people reuse passwords across services.
Example A password leaked from an old forum breach in 2019 is still being tried against banking logins today — why reused passwords stay dangerous for years.

title: Glossary — Security, Compliance & AI Terms | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) Attack An attack where someone secretly intercepts, and potentially alters, communication between two parties who believe they're communicating directly with each other.
Example Connecting to a fake "Free Airport WiFi" hotspot set up by an attacker, who can then see every unencrypted page visited during that session.
Business Email Compromise (BEC) A targeted scam, often impersonating an executive or vendor, that tricks an employee

content:

The questions people actually ask us.
Practical questions — cost, timelines, "do we need this" — plus the common challenges teams run into during implementation, across every practice. For term definitions, see the Glossary ; for step-by-step requirements, see each practice's checklists.
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , Founder & CTO, VVnT SeQuor · Last reviewed October 2026

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
All segments (158) Cybersecurity & Cyber Assurance (20) ISO & Compliance Implementation (20) Privacy & Data Protection (20) Accessibility & Inclusive Product Engineering (19) GenAI & Agentic AI Development (20) AI Testing & Evaluations (19) Digital Testing & Automation (20) Strategic IT & Architecture Advisory (20)
Cybersecurity & Cyber Assurance
How much does a penetration test typically cost?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
How much does a penetration test typically cost?
Cost varies by scope (a single web app vs. a full network vs. a whole organization) and depth (black-box vs. white-box) — from a focused few-day engagement to a multi-week assessment for larger environments. Get a scoped quote rather than relying on a generic number. Do we need a VAPT if we already run automated vulnerability scans?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Yes. Automated scanning catches known, signature-based issues; a VAPT adds human-led, context-aware exploitation attempts — including business-logic flaws — that scanners can't replicate. How often should we run a penetration test?
At least annually for most organizations, plus after any significant infrastructure or application change, and increasingly paired with continuous, lighter-touch testing in between. Is cyber insurance a substitute for security controls?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: No. Insurers increasingly require evidence of baseline controls — MFA, patching, backups, incident response — before binding a policy or paying out a claim, so insurance supplements a security programme rather than replacing one. Do small businesses really need to worry about non-human identity risk?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Yes. Even a small environment typically runs more service accounts, API keys and automation scripts than human users, and these are often the least monitored, most over-privileged accounts in the environment. What's a reasonable first step if we've never had a security assessment?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Start with a lightweight gap assessment against a recognized framework, such as CIS Controls or NIST CSF, to find the highest-risk gaps — rather than jumping straight to a full VAPT or certification effort. What's the difference between a penetration test and a red team exercise?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: A penetration test targets a defined scope — an app, a network segment — to find and demonstrate as many exploitable flaws as practical within a set timeframe. A red team exercise simulates a realistic adversary pursuing a specific objective (like reaching sensitive data) stealthily, testing detection and response as much as the technical defenses themselves. Do we have to remediate every finding, even low-severity ones?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Not immediately, but every finding needs a documented decision — fix, accept the risk, or compensate with another control. Unaddressed low-severity findings are a common audit red flag precisely because "we'll get to it" so often means "we never did." Is a web application firewall (WAF) enough to protect a public-facing app?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: No. A WAF blocks known attack patterns at the network edge, but it doesn't fix the underlying vulnerable code, and sophisticated or novel attacks can bypass it entirely. It's a useful compensating control, not a substitute for secure development and testing. How should we scope a penetration test — black-box, grey-box or white-box?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Grey-box (testers get some internal context, like a standard user account) usually gives the best balance of realism and depth for most organizations. Pure black-box is more realistic but can burn engagement time on reconnaissance; white-box (full source/architecture access) is best for deep assessments of a specific high-risk system. What's a reasonable SLA for patching a critical vulnerability?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Most mature programmes target critical, actively-exploited vulnerabilities within 24–72 hours and other critical findings within 2 weeks, with longer windows for high/medium severity — but the number matters less than having a documented SLA at all and tracking adherence to it. Do we need our own SOC, or is a managed detection and response (MDR) service enough?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Most small and mid-size organizations are better served by an MDR/SOC-as-a-service provider — 24/7 in-house monitoring is expensive to staff well. Build an internal SOC only once scale and risk genuinely justify the dedicated headcount.
Common challenges & how to avoid them
Security treated as a one-time project, not an ongoing programme
A single VAPT or audit creates a false sense of "done," when real risk keeps changing as systems, staff and threats evolve.

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
How to avoid it Budget for continuous testing, monitoring and periodic reassessment, not a single point-in-time event.
Over-privileged service accounts going unnoticed
Non-human identities multiply faster than anyone tracks them, and each one often gets broad access "to be safe."
How to avoid it Run a periodic access review specifically for service accounts and API keys, not just human users.
Alert fatigue drowning out real incidents

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Alert fatigue drowning out real incidents
Poorly tuned SIEM and monitoring tools generate so many low-value alerts that real threats get missed in the noise.
How to avoid it Invest in tuning and prioritization before adding more detection tools on top.
No tested incident response plan
Many organizations have a written IR plan that's never been rehearsed, so the first real test happens during an actual breach.

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
How to avoid it Run at least one tabletop exercise a year, and update the plan based on what it reveals.
No real asset inventory, so parts of the attack surface stay invisible
Shadow IT, forgotten subdomains and unmanaged cloud resources accumulate outside any security review — you can't protect what you don't know exists.
How to avoid it Maintain a living asset inventory fed by automated discovery, not a spreadsheet updated once a year.
Patch management stalls for fear of breaking production

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Patch management stalls for fear of breaking production
Teams delay applying fixes because a past patch once caused an outage, so "stability" quietly wins over "secure."
How to avoid it Patch in a staged environment first with a fast rollback plan, so speed and stability stop being a trade-off.
MFA treated as the finish line instead of one layer
Push-bombing and MFA-fatigue attacks exploit the fact that many teams stop hardening identity once MFA is switched on.

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
How to avoid it Pair MFA with phishing-resistant methods and anomaly-based login monitoring, not a single static factor.
Findings get reported but remediation is never actually tracked to closure
A report full of findings creates the appearance of progress, but without a tracked remediation backlog, the same issues reappear in next year's test.
How to avoid it Feed every finding into a tracked backlog with an owner and due date, and re-test against it, not just against the original scope.

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
ISO & Compliance Implementation
How much does ISO 27001 certification cost?
Costs span three buckets: internal implementation effort, any external consulting support, and the certification body's audit fees. They scale with organization size and scope — most mid-size organizations should budget several months of dedicated effort alongside the direct audit fees. Can we get certified without hiring a consultant?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Yes, if you already have an experienced internal owner and reasonable security maturity. Many organizations do succeed alone, but most find a consultant pays for itself by avoiding costly mistakes in scoping and the Statement of Applicability. What happens if we fail the certification audit?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: A major nonconformity pauses certification until it's corrected and verified, usually requiring a follow-up audit. A minor nonconformity typically just needs a documented corrective action plan before certification is issued. Do we need to recertify every year?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: No. ISO certification is valid for three years, with shorter annual or 18-month surveillance audits in between to confirm the management system is still being maintained. Can one ISMS cover multiple certifications, like ISO 27001 and ISO 27701 together?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Yes. ISO 27701 is explicitly designed as an extension to an existing ISO 27001 ISMS, though it can now also be certified standalone — organizations commonly run them as one integrated management system rather than two parallel efforts. Should we pursue SOC 2 or ISO 27001 first, or do we eventually need both?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Many organizations start with whichever their most important customers or market demands first, then add the other as their customer base diversifies. Holding both isn't unusual for companies selling into both US and international enterprise markets. What's the difference between ISO 27001:2013 and the 2022 revision?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: The 2022 revision restructured Annex A from 114 controls across 14 domains into 93 controls across 4 themed groups, and added new controls reflecting modern risk — cloud security, threat intelligence, data masking and secure coding among them. Organizations certified under the old version have a transition deadline to migrate. What happens in a Stage 1 vs. Stage 2 audit?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Stage 1 is a documentation review — the auditor checks your ISMS scope, policies and Statement of Applicability are complete and ready for assessment. Stage 2 is the real test: the auditor checks for actual operating evidence that the controls you documented are genuinely being followed. Can a startup with under 20 people realistically get ISO 27001 certified?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Yes — company size doesn't determine certifiability, scope and risk do. Small teams often move faster precisely because there's less legacy process to untangle, though they do need to resource the effort seriously rather than treat it as a side project. What's the difference between a nonconformity and an observation in an audit?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: A nonconformity means a control isn't operating as required — major ones block certification until fixed and verified, minor ones need a corrective action plan. An observation flags something that isn't a current failure but could become one, and doesn't block certification, though ignoring it repeatedly often turns it into a future nonconformity. Does getting ISO 27001 certified also make us DPDPA or GDPR compliant?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: No, but it helps substantially. ISO 27001 builds the security backbone — risk management, access control, incident response — that privacy regulations assume exists, but DPDPA/GDPR add their own distinct requirements around consent, data subject rights and lawful basis that ISO 27001 doesn't cover on its own. Is SOC 2 Type I sufficient, or do we need Type II?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Type I confirms your controls are designed correctly at a single point in time; Type II confirms they actually operated effectively over a review period, typically 6–12 months. Most enterprise buyers specifically ask for Type II because it's real evidence of sustained practice, not just a documented design.
Common challenges & how to avoid them
Treating the Statement of Applicability as a formality

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Treating the Statement of Applicability as a formality
Teams mark most controls "applicable" without real justification, which an auditor will immediately probe.
How to avoid it Tie every applicability decision directly back to the risk assessment, not convenience.
Policies that exist on paper but aren't actually followed
A well-written policy with no evidence of real operational practice is one of the most common audit findings.

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
How to avoid it Build evidence-collection into daily operations, not just document creation right before the audit.
Underestimating the time to embed a genuine security culture
Certification can be achieved faster than real behavior change spreads across the organization.
How to avoid it Start staff training and awareness early, in parallel with technical control implementation — not after.
Audit fatigue from running disconnected compliance efforts

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Audit fatigue from running disconnected compliance efforts
Separate teams chasing ISO 27001, SOC 2 and sector-specific requirements independently duplicate evidence-gathering work.
How to avoid it Map overlapping controls across frameworks once, and reuse evidence across audits — a unified control framework or GRC platform helps.
Risk assessment done once at kickoff and never revisited

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Risk assessment done once at kickoff and never revisited
The risk register that drove initial control selection quietly goes stale as the business adds new systems, vendors and products.
How to avoid it Review and update the risk assessment on a defined cadence — and whenever a significant change happens, not just annually by default.
Internal audit treated as a formality right before the external one

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Internal audit treated as a formality right before the external one
A rushed, superficial internal audit misses the same gaps the external auditor will find — at a much worse time to discover them.
How to avoid it Run the internal audit early enough, and critically enough, that its findings are actually fixed before the real audit.
Evidence scattered across emails, drives and individual inboxes

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Evidence scattered across emails, drives and individual inboxes
Without a central repository, gathering audit evidence becomes a last-minute scramble that eats weeks of everyone's time.
How to avoid it Centralize evidence collection in a GRC tool or shared structure from day one, tied to each control.
New hires never actually completing security awareness training
Training gets assigned on paper during onboarding but completion is rarely tracked, so it quietly doesn't happen.

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
How to avoid it Track training completion as a hard gate, not a suggestion, and re-certify annually.
Privacy & Data Protection
Does DPDPA apply to us if we're based outside India?
Yes, if you offer goods or services to individuals in India and process their digital personal data in that context. DPDPA has extraterritorial reach similar to GDPR's, though specifics should be confirmed with counsel for your situation. What's the penalty for DPDPA non-compliance?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: DPDPA sets financial penalties that scale with the nature and severity of the breach, decided by the Data Protection Board case by case — there isn't a single fixed number, which is part of why documented, demonstrable compliance effort matters even before any incident occurs. Do we need both a DPO and a Consent Manager?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Not necessarily both. A DPO is only mandatory if you're designated a Significant Data Fiduciary; a Consent Manager is a separate, optional entity individuals can choose to manage their consents through, not something every organization needs to appoint itself. How long does it take to become DPDPA-ready from scratch?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Timelines vary widely based on how much of a data inventory, consent infrastructure and security baseline already exists. Organizations starting from nothing should budget several months for a genuine first pass, not weeks. Is anonymized data still subject to DPDPA?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
No. Once data is genuinely and irreversibly anonymized so it can never be linked back to an individual, it falls outside DPDPA's scope. Pseudonymized data, which can still be re-identified, remains regulated. What should we do first if we've never done any privacy work?
Start with a data mapping exercise — you can't assess risk, write accurate notices, or respond to a rights request for data you haven't inventoried. Do we need separate consent for every single processing purpose?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content: Generally yes — DPDPA requires consent to be specific and granular, not one broad blanket acceptance covering unrelated purposes. Bundling marketing consent with, say, account-creation consent is a common compliance gap. When do we need to do a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)?

title: Questions & Challenges | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Before any processing activity that's likely to pose a significant risk to individuals — large-scale sensitive data processing, new tracking technology, profiling with legal or similar effects. Doing it before launch, not after, is what makes it useful. Does DPDPA restrict transferring data outside India?
DPDPA takes a more permissive approach than GDPR — cross-border transfer is generally allowed except to countries the government specifically restricts, rather than requiring a tra

Frequently asked questions
How often should we run a VAPT?
An annual penetration test alone is increasingly insufficient — most teams now pair an annual deep assessment with continuous or quarterly lighter-touch testing and automated scanning in between. What's the difference between black-box and grey-box testing?

title: Pre-VAPT Readiness / Scoping Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Black-box testing simulates an attacker with no prior knowledge of your systems; grey-box gives the tester some internal knowledge (like valid credentials), simulating an insider or a post-compromise scenario — useful for testing deeper, not just perimeter, defenses.

Frequently asked questions
How many vendors actually need a full assessment?
Not all of them — tiering by data sensitivity and system access lets you focus deep assessment on your highest-risk vendors and use lighter-touch checks for the rest, which is what makes a programme scale. Is a signed questionnaire enough evidence?

title: Vendor / Third-Party Risk Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
For lower-tier vendors, often yes. For vendors with access to sensitive data or critical systems, request independent evidence — a current SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certificate — rather than relying solely on self-attestation.

title: Regulatory Change Tracker | VVnT SeQuor
content:
No form required. This tracker is free to read and reference directly from this page — dates are tracked here as regulations evolve, so bookmark rather than download a static copy.
ISO/IEC 42001 — AI Management System
Status What it means Applies to
Published ISO/IEC 42001 is the first certifiable international standard for an AI Management System (AIMS), covering governance, risk management and lifecycle controls for AI. Organizations that develop, provide or significantly use AI systems.

title: Regulatory Change Tracker | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Ongoing Certification is voluntary but increasingly requested in enterprise procurement and vendor due diligence for AI-enabled products. Vendors selling AI-enabled products into regulated or risk-sensitive buyers.
EU AI Act — phased obligations
Phase What it requires Applies to
Feb 2025 Prohibited AI practices banned; AI-literacy obligations begin for providers and deployers. Any organization placing AI systems on the EU market or using them in the EU.

title: Regulatory Change Tracker | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Aug 2025 Obligations for general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers take effect — transparency and technical documentation duties. Providers of general-purpose AI models used in or affecting the EU.
Aug 2026 The fullest obligations apply to high-risk AI systems — conformity assessment, risk management, human oversight. Providers and deployers of AI systems classified high-risk under the Act.
EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)
Phase What it requires Applies to

title: Regulatory Change Tracker | VVnT SeQuor
content:
EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)
Phase What it requires Applies to
Sept 2026 Reporting obligations for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents begin to apply. Manufacturers of products with digital elements sold in the EU.
Dec 2027 Full application of the CRA's cybersecurity requirements, including conformity assessment for in-scope products. Manufacturers, importers and distributors of products with digital elements in the EU.
Frequently asked questions

title: Regulatory Change Tracker | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Frequently asked questions
Do these regulations apply if we're not based in the EU?
The EU AI Act and Cyber Resilience Act apply based on where products and AI systems are placed on the market or used — not where the provider is headquartered — so a non-EU organization selling into the EU can still be in scope. Does ISO 42001 certification satisfy EU AI Act obligations?

title: Regulatory Change Tracker | VVnT SeQuor
content:
It can support compliance by demonstrating a structured AI governance process, but it isn't a substitute for the Act's specific legal requirements — treat the two as complementary, not interchangeable.

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
0/7
1.1 A named owner is accountable for GDPR compliance, with a documented reporting line to leadership Art. 5(2) Accountability (Art. 5(2)) means being able to demonstrate compliance, not just claim it. How to verify this →
Test procedure Ask who owns GDPR compliance day-to-day and confirm it matches an organization chart or RACI, not just a verbal answer.
Practical example / evidence RACI matrix or org chart naming the privacy owner and their reporting line

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
1.2 A data protection policy suite exists, approved and reviewed on a defined cadence Art. 24 Covers the full suite — data protection policy, retention, breach response, rights-handling, vendor management. How to verify this →
Test procedure Check approval dates and the review cadence against the policy's own stated review interval.
Practical example / evidence Approved policy suite with version history and review dates

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
1.3 A register of processing activities is actively maintained, not a one-time exercise High risk Art. 30 A RoPA built once for an audit and never touched again is the single most common accountability gap. How to verify this →
Test procedure Check the RoPA's last-updated date against a recent change to systems or vendors.
Practical example / evidence Records of Processing Activities (RoPA) with a visible update history

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
1.4 Compliance evidence (DPIAs, processor agreements, training logs, incident records) is retained and retrievable When a regulator asks, you need to produce this quickly — not reconstruct it. How to verify this →
Test procedure Pick one processing activity and ask for its full evidence trail on the spot.
Practical example / evidence Evidence repository or shared drive structure mapped to each processing activity

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
1.5 GDPR obligations are mapped against other applicable regimes (DPDPA, CCPA, sector rules) in one register Operating in multiple jurisdictions without a single register leads to duplicated or contradicted controls. How to verify this →
Test procedure Review the cross-regime mapping document for overlap and conflicts between GDPR and other applicable laws.
Practical example / evidence Cross-regime obligations register or mapping matrix

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
1.6 Data protection is on a standing agenda for a leadership or risk committee Evidence that privacy risk reaches people with budget authority, not just the privacy team. How to verify this →
Test procedure Review committee minutes for recurring data-protection agenda items.
Practical example / evidence Committee charter and minutes showing recurring privacy agenda items

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
1.7 Exceptions and risk acceptances against GDPR controls are logged, approved and time-bound Low risk An undocumented exception is indistinguishable from a gap when a regulator reviews it. How to verify this →
Test procedure Sample the exceptions log and confirm each entry has an approver, rationale and review date.
Practical example / evidence Exceptions/risk-acceptance log with approver and expiry date

Lawful basis & records of processing
Article 6 and 30 — the foundation everything else sits on.
0/8
2.1 Every processing activity has a documented lawful basis under Article 6 High risk Art. 6 One of six bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task or legitimate interests. How to verify this →

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Test procedure Sample 5 processing activities from the RoPA and confirm each cites a specific Art. 6 basis, not a blanket default.
Practical example / evidence RoPA entries showing lawful basis per processing activity
2.2 Legitimate interests relied upon are backed by a documented balancing test Art. 6(1)(f) "Legitimate interests" without a written balancing test is the basis regulators challenge most often. How to verify this →

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Test procedure For each activity relying on legitimate interests, check for a dated balancing-test document.
Practical example / evidence Legitimate Interests Assessment (LIA) per relevant processing activity
2.3 Special category data (health, biometric, religious, etc.) has a valid Article 9 condition on top of its Article 6 basis High risk Art. 9 Special category data needs both an Art. 6 basis and a separate Art. 9 condition — a frequently missed second step. How to verify this →

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Test procedure For any special category data in the RoPA, confirm both an Art. 6 basis and an Art. 9 condition are recorded.
Practical example / evidence RoPA entries showing both Art. 6 basis and Art. 9 condition where applicable
2.4 The RoPA records purpose, categories of data, recipients, third-country transfers and retention period per activity Art. 30 A RoPA missing retention periods or recipients isn't audit-ready even if it technically exists. How to verify this →

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Test procedure Check the RoPA template fields against the full list Art. 30 requires.
Practical example / evidence RoPA template/export showing all required fields populated
2.5 Processing of children's data (where applicable) has age-verification and parental-consent mechanisms Art. 8 Relevant wherever your product could reasonably be used by minors. How to verify this →
Test procedure Review the age-gate/consent flow for any product surface reachable by minors.

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Practical example / evidence Age-verification and parental-consent flow documentation
2.6 Purpose limitation is enforced — data isn't reused for a new purpose without re-assessing the lawful basis A common drift: data collected for one purpose quietly gets used for another (e.g. analytics data used for marketing). How to verify this →
Test procedure Pick a dataset and trace every system that consumes it against its originally stated purpose.

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Practical example / evidence Data-flow map showing purpose per downstream use
2.7 Data minimization is applied — only data genuinely needed for the stated purpose is collected Art. 5(1)(c) Over-collection increases both breach exposure and your Art. 5(1)(c) compliance burden. How to verify this →
Test procedure Review a sample intake form or API payload against the purpose it serves for unnecessary fields.

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Practical example / evidence Data minimization review for at least one major collection point
2.8 Retention schedules are defined per data category and enforced technically, not just on paper Medium risk A written retention policy that isn't enforced by a deletion job is not evidence of compliance. How to verify this →
Test procedure Pick a data category past its stated retention period and confirm it was actually deleted or justified as still needed.

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Practical example / evidence Retention schedule plus evidence of an automated or scheduled deletion process

Consent & transparency
Article 7 and Articles 12–14 — what has to be true before and at the point of collection.
0/7
3.1 Consent capture is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous — no pre-ticked boxes High risk Art. 7 Pre-ticked boxes, bundled consent and silence all fail the GDPR consent standard. How to verify this →

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Test procedure Walk through the actual consent UI/flow and check for pre-ticked boxes or bundled permissions.
Practical example / evidence Screenshots or recording of the live consent flow
3.2 Consent is as easy to withdraw as it was to give, with no penalty for withdrawing Art. 7(3) A consent flow with a one-click opt-in and a multi-step opt-out fails Art. 7(3). How to verify this →

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Test procedure Attempt to withdraw consent through the actual product and time/step-count it against the opt-in flow.
Practical example / evidence Withdrawal flow walkthrough, compared step-for-step with the opt-in flow
3.3 Consent records (who, when, what version of notice, what was agreed) are retained as proof You need to be able to prove consent was given, not just that a checkbox exists today. How to verify this →

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Test procedure Pull a consent record for a specific individual and confirm it has a timestamp and notice version.
Practical example / evidence Consent log/database with timestamp and notice-version fields
3.4 Privacy notices disclose identity/contact details, purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention and rights Art. 13-14 Articles 13–14 specify an exact list of disclosures — a generic privacy policy often misses several. How to verify this →

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Test procedure Check the live privacy notice against the full Art. 13/14 disclosure checklist line by line.
Practical example / evidence Current privacy notice mapped against the Art. 13/14 disclosure list
3.5 Notices are presented at the point of collection, not buried in a separate legal page only Layered/just-in-time notices at the collection point are expected practice, not just a nice-to-have. How to verify this →

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Test procedure Check whether a notice or link to one appears at the actual point data is collected (form, API, SDK).
Practical example / evidence Screenshot of the notice or notice link at the point of collection
3.6 Privacy notices are reviewed and updated whenever processing purposes or recipients change A notice that doesn't match current data flows is a transparency gap even if it was accurate once. How to verify this →

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Test procedure Compare the current notice's stated recipients/purposes against the current RoPA.
Practical example / evidence Change log showing the notice was updated alongside a processing change
3.7 Cookie and tracking consent is layered — strictly necessary cookies load before consent, others wait Medium risk Non-essential trackers firing before consent is one of the most commonly enforced GDPR/ePrivacy gaps. How to verify this →

title: GDPR Readiness Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Test procedure Load the site with a clean browser profile and inspect network requests before any consent action.
Practical example / evidence Network trace showing non-essential cookies/trackers blocked pre-consent

4.3 Encryption protects ePHI at rest, or an equivalent documented alternative measure is in place High risk §164.312(a)(2)(iv) Encryption is addressable, not required outright — but where not implemented, the alternative and its rationale must be documented. How to verify this →

content:

Frequently asked questions
Does an accessibility overlay satisfy these checklist items?

title: WCAG 2.2 Audit + VPAT/ACR Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Does an accessibility overlay satisfy these checklist items?
No. Overlays operate on top of the page and can't fix underlying markup, keyboard operability or focus-management issues — they're widely found not to achieve real WCAG conformance and don't reduce legal risk. Do we need WCAG 2.2 or is 2.1 still acceptable?

title: WCAG 2.2 Audit + VPAT/ACR Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content: Most current regulatory references point to WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 depending on jurisdiction and when the requirement was set; 2.2 is the more current standard and includes criteria (like focus visibility and accessible authentication) that address real, frequently-cited failures — worth meeting even where only 2.1 is formally required. What's the difference between a VPAT and an ACR?

title: WCAG 2.2 Audit + VPAT/ACR Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
VPAT is the template format; once filled in for your specific product, the completed document is called an Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR). People often use the terms interchangeably.

title: AI Agent Guardrail & Red-Team Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Frequently asked questions
Where should human approval checkpoints go?
At points that are high-consequence, hard to reverse, or legally sensitive — financial transactions, data deletion, external communications — rather than at every single step, which defeats the purpose of agentic automation. Is red-teaming a one-time pre-launch activity?

title: AI Agent Guardrail & Red-Team Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
No — model updates, new tools and new user populations all change the attack surface. Red-teaming should recur, especially after any change to the agent's tools, permissions or underlying model.

Frequently asked questions
Can LLM-as-a-judge fully replace human evaluation?
It scales evaluation well beyond what manual review alone can cover, but it has its own blind spots and biases — most mature pipelines combine LLM-as-a-judge scoring with periodic human review, especially for safety-critical categories. How often should evaluation run after launch?

title: LLM / Chatbot Evaluation Checklist | VVnT SeQuor
content:
Continuously, ideally — model providers update models, your own prompts and retrieved data drift, and a continuous evaluation pipeline catches quality regressions that a single pre-launch evaluation would miss entirely.

title: Why an Annual Penetration Test Isn’t Enough Anymore
content:
Cybersecurity & Cyber Assurance
Why an Annual Penetration Test Isn't Enough Anymore
A penetration test report is a snapshot. The moment you ship your next release, deploy a new integration, or add a dependency, that snapshot stops describing your actual attack surface.
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , Founder & CTO, VVnT SeQuor ·
May 19, 2026 ·
2 min read
In this article
01
The compliance checkbox problem
Most organizations run VAPT once a year because a customer, auditor or regulator asks for it.
02

title: Why an Annual Penetration Test Isn’t Enough Anymore
content:
02
What continuous security testing actually adds
Continuous security testing doesn't replace a formal VAPT engagement — it closes the…
03
Where this fits for third-party assessments
Many clients come to this from a third-party assessment requirement — a customer or partner…
The compliance checkbox problem

title: Why an Annual Penetration Test Isn’t Enough Anymore
content:
The compliance checkbox problem
Most organizations run VAPT once a year because a customer, auditor or regulator asks for it. That satisfies the checkbox, but it doesn't reflect how modern applications actually change. A typical engineering team ships code weekly, sometimes daily. Cloud configurations drift. Third-party libraries get patched — or don't. By month three of a twelve-month VAPT cycle, the report on file is already describing a system that no longer exists.

title: Why an Annual Penetration Test Isn’t Enough Anymore
content:
Treat continuous testing as the layer that runs between pentests, not a replacement for them — most mature programmes run both.
What continuous security testing actually adds
Continuous security testing doesn't replace a formal VAPT engagement — it closes the gap between them. In practice, that means:
Automated SAST/DAST/IAST scanning wired into the CI/CD pipeline, so a vulnerable dependency or an injection flaw is flagged before merge, not a year later.

title: Why an Annual Penetration Test Isn’t Enough Anymore
content:
Scoped, targeted re-tests after major releases or infrastructure changes, rather than waiting for the next annual cycle.
Cloud security posture monitoring that catches misconfigurations (open storage buckets, over-permissioned IAM roles) as they happen.
DevSecOps practices — threat modeling at design time, security champions embedded in engineering teams — so security is a property of the build, not an audit bolted on afterward.
Where this fits for third-party assessments

title: Why an Annual Penetration Test Isn’t Enough Anymore
content:
Where this fits for third-party assessments
Many clients come to this from a third-party assessment requirement — a customer or partner needs assurance that your security posture is sound before they'll sign. A single stale VAPT report increasingly doesn't satisfy that bar. What does is being able to show a continuously tested posture: recent scan results, a documented remediation SLA, and a clear testing cadence tied to your release cycle.

title: Why an Annual Penetration Test Isn’t Enough Anymore
content:
The practical shift: treat VAPT as the deep, periodic audit, and continuous testing as the day-to-day discipline that keeps the gap between audits small. Neither one substitutes for the other.
Getting started without boiling the ocean

title: Why an Annual Penetration Test Isn’t Enough Anymore
content:
Getting started without boiling the ocean
You don't need to overhaul your entire pipeline in one sprint. A reasonable sequence: get SAST running in CI first (cheapest to adopt, catches the most common classes of bugs), add DAST against a staging environment next, layer in cloud posture monitoring, and only then formalize a DevSecOps operating model with champions and threat modeling. Each step is independently useful, and you stop whenever the residual risk is acceptable for your context.

title: Why an Annual Penetration Test Isn’t Enough Anymore
content:
Frequently asked questions
Does continuous security testing replace our annual VAPT requirement?
No. Most compliance frameworks and customer contracts still require a formal, periodic VAPT engagement from a qualified third party. Continuous testing supplements that by catching issues in between audit cycles — it doesn't satisfy the audit requirement on its own.
What's the difference between SAST, DAST and IAST?

title: Why an Annual Penetration Test Isn’t Enough Anymore
content:
What's the difference between SAST, DAST and IAST?
SAST (static analysis) scans source code without running it, catching issues early in development. DAST (dynamic analysis) tests a running application from the outside, the way an attacker would. IAST (interactive analysis) instruments the running application to combine the visibility of both. Most mature pipelines use some combination of all three.
How often should a third-party assessment (3PAA) actually be refreshed?

title: Why an Annual Penetration Test Isn’t Enough Anymore
content:
How often should a third-party assessment (3PAA) actually be refreshed?
It depends on your risk profile and what your customers or regulators require, but annually is a common minimum, with a scoped re-test after any major architecture or infrastructure change in between.

ISO & Compliance Implementation
ISO 27001 Certification: A Realistic Timeline and Readiness Checklist
"How long will ISO 27001 take?" is almost always the first question, and the honest answer is: it depends more on your organization's readiness than on the standard itself.
Reviewed by Parveen Kumar Arora , Founder & CEO, VVnT SeQuor ·
April 20, 2026 ·
2 min read
In this article
01
A realistic timeline
For a mid-sized organization starting close to zero formal information security management, a…

content:
02
The readiness checklist

03
Where implementations stall
The most common reason a certification timeline slips isn't the audit itself —…
A realistic timeline

title: ISO 27001 Certification: A Realistic Timeline and…
content:
A realistic timeline
For a mid-sized organization starting close to zero formal information security management, a typical path to certification runs three to six months of implementation, followed by a Stage 1 and Stage 2 audit from an accredited certification body. Organizations with existing security practices — access controls, backup procedures, incident response, even if undocumented — can move faster, because the gap assessment finds less to build from scratch.

title: ISO 27001 Certification: A Realistic Timeline and…
content:
A realistic run — most of the elapsed time sits in remediation and evidence-gathering, not in the audits themselves.
The readiness checklist
Before you can realistically schedule a Stage 1 audit, you need:
A completed gap assessment against Annex A controls, scoped to your actual ISMS boundary.
A risk register with identified assets, threats, and documented treatment decisions — not a template filled in once and forgotten.

title: ISO 27001 Certification: A Realistic Timeline and…
content:
Core ISMS documentation: information security policy, Statement of Applicability (SoA), risk treatment plan, and the mandatory procedures the standard requires.
At least one internal audit cycle completed, with findings tracked to closure.
A management review meeting on record, showing leadership is actually engaged with the ISMS, not just sponsoring it on paper.

title: ISO 27001 Certification: A Realistic Timeline and…
content:
Evidence that controls are operating, not just documented — access review logs, training completion records, incident response drill results.
Where implementations stall

title: ISO 27001 Certification: A Realistic Timeline and…
content:
Where implementations stall
The most common reason a certification timeline slips isn't the audit itself — it's evidence. Writing a policy is fast; generating three months of consistent operational evidence that the policy is actually being followed takes exactly three months, and there's no way to compress that. Organizations that try to rush straight from policy-writing to Stage 2 without an operating history typically get non-conformities for exactly this reason.

title: ISO 27001 Certification: A Realistic Timeline and…
content:
Rule of thumb: budget at least one full quarter of "live" operation under the ISMS — controls running, evidence accumulating — between finishing documentation and scheduling Stage 2. That operating history is what the auditor is actually there to verify.
SOC 2 alongside ISO 27001

title: ISO 27001 Certification: A Realistic Timeline and…
content:
SOC 2 alongside ISO 27001
If you're also pursuing SOC 2 — common for SaaS vendors selling into the US — there's substantial control overlap with ISO 27001 Annex A. Mapping both frameworks' requirements together from the start avoids duplicating evidence-collection work later.

Frequently asked questions
Can we get certified faster if we pay for an expedited audit?
The certification body's audit scheduling can sometimes be expedited, but the operating-evidence requirement can't be — auditors are specifically checking that controls have been running long enough to generate a track record, which an expedited booking doesn't shortcut.
Do we need ISO 27001 and ISO 27701 separately, or can they be combined?

title: ISO 27001 Certification: A Realistic Timeline and…
content:
Do we need ISO 27001 and ISO 27701 separately, or can they be combined?
They can be implemented together efficiently, since ISO 27701 (the privacy information management extension) builds directly on an ISO 27001 ISMS. Organizations with both security and privacy obligations — most that handle personal data — often implement them as one combined programme.
What happens after certification — is it a one-time event?

title: ISO 27001 Certification: A Realistic Timeline and…
content:
What happens after certification — is it a one-time event?
No. Certification is maintained through annual surveillance audits and a full recertification audit every three years, so the ISMS has to keep operating, not just exist at the point of the original audit.

content:
Privacy & Data Protection
DPDPA Compliance: A Practical Checklist for Indian Businesses
India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA) changes what "consent" and "data handling" mean for any business processing personal data of individuals in India — and the operational work to get ready is more involved than it sounds from the headlines.
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , Founder & CTO, VVnT SeQuor ·
April 27, 2026 ·
2 min read
In this article
01
Start with data mapping, not policy-writing

title: DPDPA Compliance: A Practical Checklist for Indian…
content:
2 min read
In this article
01

The instinct is to start with a privacy policy.
02
The operational checklist
Data inventory and flow mapping across all systems, including vendor and sub-processor…
03
Where GDPR-aligned organizations have a head start
If you've already built a GDPR programme — common for companies serving EU customers…
Start with data mapping, not policy-writing

title: DPDPA Compliance: A Practical Checklist for Indian…
content:
Start with data mapping, not policy-writing
The instinct is to start with a privacy policy. The more useful starting point is a data map: what personal data you actually collect, where it lives, who inside (and outside) the organization can access it, how long you keep it, and which third parties it flows to. Without that map, every other DPDPA requirement — consent design, purpose limitation, breach notification — is being built on a guess rather than a fact.

title: DPDPA Compliance: A Practical Checklist for Indian…
content:
Data mapping comes first because every other control — consent, retention, breach response — depends on knowing where the data actually is.
The operational checklist
Data inventory and flow mapping across all systems, including vendor and sub-processor relationships.
Consent mechanisms that are specific, informed, and as easy to withdraw as to give — a pre-ticked box or a buried settings page won't hold up.

title: DPDPA Compliance: A Practical Checklist for Indian…
content:
A clear, itemized notice at the point of collection explaining what's collected and why, in plain language.
Defined data retention periods per data category, with a process to actually delete data once the purpose is served.
A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) process for higher-risk processing activities, particularly involving children's data or large-scale profiling.

title: DPDPA Compliance: A Practical Checklist for Indian…
content:
A breach detection and notification procedure, including who tells the Data Protection Board and affected individuals, and on what timeline.
Vendor contracts updated to flow down DPDPA obligations to any processor handling data on your behalf.
Where GDPR-aligned organizations have a head start

title: DPDPA Compliance: A Practical Checklist for Indian…
content:
Where GDPR-aligned organizations have a head start
If you've already built a GDPR programme — common for companies serving EU customers — a meaningful share of that work (data mapping, DPIAs, breach procedures) transfers directly. The DPDPA isn't identical to GDPR, but the operational muscle of inventorying data and designing consent properly is the same muscle.

title: DPDPA Compliance: A Practical Checklist for Indian…
content:
Not legal advice: this is a practical implementation checklist, not a legal opinion. DPDPA interpretation for your specific data flows and sector should be confirmed with qualified counsel; our role is implementing the technical and process controls those interpretations require.
ISO 27701 as the operating backbone

title: DPDPA Compliance: A Practical Checklist for Indian…
content:
ISO 27701 as the operating backbone
Many organizations find it easier to run DPDPA compliance as an extension of an existing ISMS, using ISO 27701's Privacy Information Management System (PIMS) structure to organize the data mapping, risk assessment and control evidence DPDPA readiness requires, rather than building a separate, parallel privacy programme from scratch.

Frequently asked questions
Does DPDPA apply to us if we only process data within India?

title: DPDPA Compliance: A Practical Checklist for Indian…
content:
Does DPDPA apply to us if we only process data within India?
DPDPA applies broadly to processing of digital personal data within India, and to processing outside India where it relates to offering goods or services to individuals in India. Scope for your specific operations should be confirmed with counsel.
Is a DPIA mandatory for every business?

title: DPDPA Compliance: A Practical Checklist for Indian…
content:
Is a DPIA mandatory for every business?
Not for every processing activity, but it's expected for higher-risk processing — large-scale data use, data involving children, or activities that could significantly affect individuals. Building a DPIA process in now, even a lightweight one, avoids scrambling later.
How is DPDPA different from GDPR?

title: DPDPA Compliance: A Practical Checklist for Indian…
content:
How is DPDPA different from GDPR?
They share a similar underlying logic (lawful basis for processing, individual rights, breach notification) but differ in specifics — consent mechanics, the role of "Consent Managers," and penalty structure. Treat DPDPA as its own framework rather than assuming GDPR compliance automatically covers it.

content:
Accessibility & Inclusive Product Engineering
WCAG 2.2 and the Business Case for Accessibility
Accessibility conversations usually start with risk — a lawsuit, an audit, a procurement requirement — but the stronger long-term argument is the one that rarely gets made: accessible products reach more people and cost less to maintain.
Reviewed by Parveen Kumar Arora , Founder & CEO, VVnT SeQuor ·
April 13, 2026 ·
2 min read
In this article
01
What changed in WCAG 2.2

title: WCAG 2.2 and the Business Case for Accessibility
content:
April 13, 2026 ·
2 min read
In this article
01
What changed in WCAG 2.2
WCAG 2.2 added nine new success criteria on top of 2.1, with a particular focus on cognitive…
02
The market you're not reaching
Roughly one in six people globally live with some form of disability, and that doesn't count…
03
The compliance landscape
Section 508 governs US federal procurement — if you sell to US government agencies,…
What changed in WCAG 2.2

title: WCAG 2.2 and the Business Case for Accessibility
content:
What changed in WCAG 2.2
WCAG 2.2 added nine new success criteria on top of 2.1, with a particular focus on cognitive accessibility, mobile interaction patterns, and authentication. Focus Not Obscured, Dragging Movements, Target Size (Minimum), and Accessible Authentication are the ones most product teams encounter first — they affect everyday UI decisions like modal placement, drag-and-drop interactions, and tap target sizing, not just screen-reader edge cases.

title: WCAG 2.2 and the Business Case for Accessibility
content:
WCAG's four POUR principles — every success criterion in the standard, including what changed in 2.2, maps back to one of these four.
The market you're not reaching

title: WCAG 2.2 and the Business Case for Accessibility
content: Roughly one in six people globally live with some form of disability, and that doesn't count the much larger group affected by situational or temporary limitations — a broken arm, bright sunlight on a phone screen, a noisy environment that makes audio content unusable. Accessible design decisions — sufficient contrast, resizable text, captions, logical keyboard navigation — make products easier to use for everyone in those conditions, not just permanent assistive-technology users.

title: WCAG 2.2 and the Business Case for Accessibility
content:
The compliance landscape
Section 508 governs US federal procurement — if you sell to US government agencies, conformance isn't optional.
The ADA has been applied to websites and apps through litigation even without a specific digital-accessibility statute, making WCAG conformance the de facto legal standard referenced in settlements.
A growing number of enterprise RFPs now require a current VPAT® / Accessibility Conformance Report before a vendor can even be evaluated.

title: WCAG 2.2 and the Business Case for Accessibility
content:
India's GIGW guidelines apply a similar WCAG-aligned bar for government and PSU-facing digital properties.
The remediation math: fixing a contrast ratio or a missing form label during design review costs a design tweak. Fixing it after launch, discovered through a complaint or an audit, costs an engineering sprint, a re-test cycle, and often a VPAT re-issue. Accessibility debt compounds exactly like technical debt.
Where to start if you're at zero

title: WCAG 2.2 and the Business Case for Accessibility
content:
Where to start if you're at zero
An initial WCAG audit against a representative set of key user flows — not the whole site at once — gives you a prioritized, evidence-backed remediation list rather than a vague sense that "accessibility needs work." From there, VPAT® / ACR preparation turns that audit into the document your enterprise customers and procurement teams are actually asking for.
