The decisions a CIO actually needs to make

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content:
03
The decisions a CIO actually needs to make
Build versus buy versus assemble: commercial IDP products, open-source frameworks, and fully…
The problem platform engineering actually solves

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content: As organizations scale microservices, cloud infrastructure, and DevOps practices, individual engineering teams end up repeatedly solving the same infrastructure, deployment, and tooling problems independently — each team configuring its own CI/CD pipeline, provisioning its own cloud resources, managing its own observability setup, often inconsistently and redundantly. An internal developer platform (IDP) centralizes this into a self-service layer: a golden path that lets product engineering

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content: this into a self-service layer: a golden path that lets product engineering teams deploy, configure, and operate their services without needing deep infrastructure expertise or repeatedly solving solved problems.

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content:
A platform that skips the last item — a clear interface to product teams — tends to drift into a side project that nobody outside the platform team can rely on.
What a good internal developer platform actually provides
Self-service provisioning — a developer can spin up a new service, database, or environment through a defined, governed path, without filing a ticket and waiting on a platform team.

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content:
Golden-path templates that bake in your organization's security, compliance, and operational standards by default, so following the easy path is also the compliant path.
Consistent observability, logging, and incident response tooling across services, rather than each team choosing (and maintaining) its own.
A clear API or interface between the platform team and product teams, so the platform evolves as a product with its own roadmap and users, not an ad hoc collection of scripts and runbooks.

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content:
The decisions a CIO actually needs to make
Build versus buy versus assemble: commercial IDP products, open-source frameworks, and fully custom-built platforms each have different cost, flexibility, and lock-in trade-offs — and the right choice depends heavily on your existing infrastructure maturity and team size.

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content: Dedicated platform team or not: a platform built and maintained as a side project by infrastructure engineers with other responsibilities rarely reaches the reliability and usability bar needed for genuine adoption. Treating platform engineering as its own product, with its own dedicated team, is usually what separates successful initiatives from abandoned ones.

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content: Adoption strategy: a platform that's mandated but not genuinely better than teams' existing workflows gets worked around. Measuring and designing for actual developer experience, not just technical completeness, determines whether adoption sticks.

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content: The ROI case has to be made in developer time, not just infrastructure cost. The primary return on platform engineering investment is engineering velocity — less time spent on undifferentiated infrastructure work, faster time from idea to deployed service — which is harder to quantify than a direct infrastructure cost saving but is usually the larger number once measured honestly through metrics like deployment frequency and lead time.

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content: Where this connects to the rest of the architecture practice

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content:
An internal developer platform is, in large part, an embodiment of your architecture governance and standards made executable — the golden paths it offers should reflect the same security, compliance, and technology principles your broader enterprise architecture practice has already defined. Platform engineering initiatives that proceed independently of architecture governance tend to encode a parallel, inconsistent set of standards, defeating much of the point.
Frequently asked questions

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content:
Frequently asked questions
Is platform engineering only relevant for large organizations?
The core problem it solves — teams repeatedly reinventing infrastructure and deployment patterns — appears earlier than most expect, often once an organization has more than a handful of engineering teams and services. The scale of investment should match organizational size, but the underlying discipline (golden paths, self-service, treating the platform as a product) applies well before enterprise scale.

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content:
How do we measure whether our internal developer platform is actually working?
Developer experience metrics (deployment frequency, lead time for changes, time to provision new environments, platform team support ticket volume) are more telling than technical completeness checklists. A platform with excellent documentation and low adoption is not succeeding, whatever its technical merits.
Does adopting a platform engineering approach require adopting a specific tool like Backstage?

title: Platform Engineering and Internal Developer Platforms…
content:
No — specific tools (Backstage and similar) are common implementation choices, but the practice is the discipline (self-service, golden paths, treating the platform as a product), not any particular tool. The right tooling choice depends on your existing stack and team capacity to build and maintain it.

Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography Planning Can't Wait
Quantum computers capable of breaking today's public-key encryption don't exist yet. The data an attacker steals and stores today, to decrypt once they do, is already being collected — which is why post-quantum planning is a today problem, not a someday one.

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content: The attack that's already happening

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content: "Harvest now, decrypt later" describes a strategy, not a prediction: an adversary intercepts and stores encrypted traffic or exfiltrated data today, betting that a sufficiently capable quantum computer will eventually be able to break the RSA or elliptic-curve encryption protecting it. For data with a long confidentiality shelf life — health records, government communications, trade secrets, anything that still matters in ten or fifteen years — that bet doesn't need quantum computing to arrive

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content: in ten or fifteen years — that bet doesn't need quantum computing to arrive soon to be worth making now.

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content: What NIST's post-quantum standards actually change

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content: NIST finalized its first set of post-quantum cryptography standards in August 2024 — ML-KEM (key encapsulation, derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber) for encryption and ML-DSA (digital signatures, derived from CRYSTALS-Dilithium) chief among them. That finalization matters because it moves post-quantum cryptography from "candidate algorithms being evaluated" to "standards vendors can actually build against" — browsers, cloud providers, and security libraries are rolling in support on a real, if

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content: cloud providers, and security libraries are rolling in support on a real, if staggered, timeline.

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content:
Most organizations skip straight to step three without ever completing step one — the inventory is slow, unglamorous work, but it's what makes every later step possible to prioritize correctly.
Where to start: a crypto inventory most organizations don't have

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content:
Where to start: a crypto inventory most organizations don't have
Most organizations cannot currently answer "where do we use RSA or ECC, and for what" without a dedicated inventory effort — cryptography is embedded in TLS configurations, VPNs, code-signing processes, and third-party libraries, rarely centrally tracked.

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content:
Prioritize by data sensitivity and confidentiality lifespan, not by system criticality alone — a system protecting data that's worthless in five years is a lower migration priority than one protecting data that needs to stay confidential for decades, even if the former is otherwise more business-critical.
Flag vendor and third-party dependencies explicitly — your own migration plan is incomplete if a critical vendor's cryptography roadmap isn't part of the picture.

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content:
A realistic migration sequence
Most guidance converges on hybrid approaches first: running classical and post-quantum algorithms together during a transition period, so a flaw discovered in the newer post-quantum algorithms doesn't leave systems with no proven fallback. Full migration to post-quantum-only cryptography follows once hybrid approaches have matured in production and vendor support is broad enough that it's not a bespoke engineering effort for every system.

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content:
This isn't a 2026 deadline problem. No regulator has set a hard post-quantum migration deadline for most industries yet. The reason to start the inventory now is that it's slow, cross-cutting work with a long tail — starting it two years before you need results is a very different position than starting it once a deadline or incident forces the pace.

Frequently asked questions
Do we need to migrate everything to post-quantum cryptography right now?

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content:
Do we need to migrate everything to post-quantum cryptography right now?
No — the realistic first step is a cryptographic inventory and a prioritized plan based on data sensitivity and confidentiality lifespan, not an immediate wholesale migration. Systems protecting long-lived sensitive data deserve earlier attention than systems protecting short-lived or already-public data.
Is post-quantum cryptography the same as quantum encryption?

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content:
Is post-quantum cryptography the same as quantum encryption?
No — post-quantum cryptography refers to classical algorithms (like ML-KEM and ML-DSA) designed to resist attacks from quantum computers, run on today's ordinary hardware. Quantum encryption (quantum key distribution) is a different, much less widely deployed approach that requires specialized hardware.
How urgent is this really, given quantum computers that can break RSA don't exist yet?

title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why Post-Quantum Cryptography…
content:
The urgency is specific to data with a long confidentiality shelf life being harvested today, not to an imminent quantum breakthrough. For data that only needs to stay confidential for a year or two, the urgency is genuinely low; for data that needs to stay confidential for a decade or more, the harvesting risk is active today regardless of when a capable quantum computer actually arrives.

content:
Cybersecurity & Cyber Assurance
Continuous Threat Exposure Management: Moving Beyond Point-in-Time Vulnerability Scans
A vulnerability scan tells you what's exposed today. It says nothing about which of those exposures an attacker could actually reach and exploit, or whether last quarter's fixes have quietly drifted back open. Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM) is the response to that gap.
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , Founder & CTO, VVnT SeQuor ·
September 2, 2026 ·
3 min read

title: Continuous Threat Exposure Management: Moving Beyond…
content:
September 2, 2026 ·
3 min read
In this article
01
What CTEM actually is
CTEM is a structured, ongoing programme — not a tool or a single scan type — for…
02
The five stages
Scoping — defining which business-critical systems, applications, and attack surfaces the…
03
Why it's different from vulnerability management
Traditional vulnerability management asks "what's vulnerable?" and generates a…
What CTEM actually is

title: Continuous Threat Exposure Management: Moving Beyond…
content:
What CTEM actually is
CTEM is a structured, ongoing programme — not a tool or a single scan type — for continuously identifying, validating, and prioritizing the exposures that matter most to a specific organization's actual attack surface. The shift it represents is from periodic, broad vulnerability counting toward continuous, narrower, context-aware exposure validation: fewer findings, but findings that are confirmed exploitable and ranked by real business impact.

title: Continuous Threat Exposure Management: Moving Beyond…
content:
CTEM runs this cycle continuously, not once — each stage feeds the next, and mobilization's results feed back into the next scoping pass.
The five stages
Scoping — defining which business-critical systems, applications, and attack surfaces the programme actually covers, rather than trying to boil the entire estate at once.

title: Continuous Threat Exposure Management: Moving Beyond…
content:
Discovery — identifying assets, vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and exposures across that defined scope, including shadow IT and unmanaged assets that standard scans often miss.
Prioritization — ranking findings by actual exploitability and business impact, not a generic CVSS severity score alone, since a critical-severity finding on an isolated, low-value system matters less than a medium-severity one on a system an attacker can actually reach.

title: Continuous Threat Exposure Management: Moving Beyond…
content:
Validation — confirming that a prioritized exposure is genuinely exploitable in your environment, often through controlled adversarial testing, before committing remediation resources to it.
Mobilization — getting the validated, prioritized findings to the teams who can actually fix them, with enough context and urgency that remediation isn't a separate, disconnected process from the assessment.
Why it's different from vulnerability management

title: Continuous Threat Exposure Management: Moving Beyond…
content:
Why it's different from vulnerability management
Traditional vulnerability management asks "what's vulnerable?" and generates a list, often thousands of findings long, with severity scores that don't reflect actual exploitability in context. CTEM asks a narrower question — "what can actually be exploited, and what would it cost us if it were?" — and treats that as a continuous cycle rather than a point-in-time report that goes stale the moment a new deployment ships.

title: Continuous Threat Exposure Management: Moving Beyond…
content:
CTEM complements continuous security testing, it doesn't replace it. Automated scanning and continuous testing (the subject of our piece on why an annual pentest isn't enough) feed the discovery stage; CTEM is the program-level structure that decides what to do with everything those tools surface.
Getting started

title: Continuous Threat Exposure Management: Moving Beyond…
content:
Getting started
Organizations with mature vulnerability management programmes already have most of the raw material CTEM needs — the gap is usually in prioritization and validation, not discovery. A realistic starting point is picking one defined, business-critical scope (not the entire estate) and running a full cycle through all five stages before expanding, rather than attempting to stand up a comprehensive CTEM programme across everything at once.
Frequently asked questions

title: Continuous Threat Exposure Management: Moving Beyond…
content:
Frequently asked questions
Is CTEM a specific product we need to buy?
No — CTEM is a programme structure, popularized by Gartner, that can be implemented with a combination of existing tools (vulnerability scanners, attack surface management, breach and attack simulation) rather than a single product. Vendors market CTEM-aligned platforms, but the discipline doesn't require starting from a specific tool.
How is CTEM different from continuous security testing in CI/CD?

title: Continuous Threat Exposure Management: Moving Beyond…
content:
How is CTEM different from continuous security testing in CI/CD?
Continuous security testing (SAST, DAST, scanning in the pipeline) is a discovery mechanism that feeds CTEM's process; CTEM is the broader programme that prioritizes, validates, and routes everything discovered, including findings that have nothing to do with code (misconfigurations, exposed assets, third-party exposures).
Do we need a dedicated team to run a CTEM programme?

title: Continuous Threat Exposure Management: Moving Beyond…
content:
Do we need a dedicated team to run a CTEM programme?
Not necessarily a new team — many organizations run CTEM as a structured process owned by existing security operations or vulnerability management staff, with validation support from internal or external penetration testing resources on an as-needed basis rather than full-time.

The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: What 100+ Sites in 23 Hours Means for Enterprise AI Governance
An AI agent, not a human operator, planned and carried out a breach that reached John Deere, SharkNinja, Cummins and more than 100 other organizations in a single 23-hour window — by compromising one shared supplier and moving on from there. Here's what actually happened, and what it changes for how enterprises govern agentic AI on both sides of the fence.

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content:
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , Founder & CTO, VVnT SeQuor ·
October 23, 2026 ·
5 min read
In this article
01
What happened
A single compromised supplier gave an autonomous agent a foothold that it used to reach 100+ downstream organizations in 23 hours.
02
Why the speed matters
Lateral movement and exploitation that used to take a skilled team weeks now runs at machine pace, around the clock, without fatigue.
03
What defenders should change

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content:
03
What defenders should change
Supply-chain scoping, decision logging and per-resource authorization gates — for your own agents as much as the attacker's.
What happened

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: Security researchers investigating a cluster of intrusions traced them back to a single entry point: a shared third-party supplier whose access was trusted by a long list of downstream customers. Once that supplier was compromised, an autonomous AI agent — not a human operator working case by case — took over the reconnaissance, credential harvesting and lateral movement needed to reach each of that supplier's customers in turn. Confirmed and suspected victims span a wide range of industrial

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: in turn. Confirmed and suspected victims span a wide range of industrial and consumer manufacturers, including John Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins, with investigators tracking signs of the same campaign touching well over 100 organizations in total. The entire sequence, from the initial supplier compromise to reaching that many downstream targets, played out in roughly 23 hours.

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: That timeline is the headline, and for good reason. Supply-chain attacks that pivot from one trusted vendor to dozens or hundreds of its customers are not new — that has been a standard, well-understood attack pattern for years. What is new here is the compression: tasks that a human-led team would plan over days and execute over weeks (scope each target, adapt the exploit, avoid detection, move to the next) were handled by an agent working through them continuously, without the natural rate

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: handled by an agent working through them continuously, without the natural rate limits of a human analyst needing sleep, context-switching, or sign-off between targets.

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content:
The distinction that matters: this was not a new category of attack. It was an old, well-understood category — shared-supplier compromise — executed at a speed that assumes a human is still the bottleneck in attacker tradecraft. That assumption no longer holds, and detection timelines built around it don't either.
Why the speed changes the defensive math

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: Most breach-detection and incident-response playbooks are built around an implicit clock: attackers take time to move laterally, defenders have a window to notice unusual activity before it reaches a second, third or hundredth target. An agent that can replicate the same exploitation playbook against each new target the moment it is identified — with no coordination overhead, no waiting on a human to approve the next step — collapses that window from days to hours. By the time a security team

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: step — collapses that window from days to hours. By the time a security team at target #1 contains the intrusion and starts asking whether anyone else who uses the same supplier might be affected, the agent may already be well into target #80.

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: This is also why the incident has become a reference point well beyond the companies directly involved. In the days since, it has pushed several bodies to act: CISA , NIST and the NSA have been working on joint guidance for responding to incidents involving rogue or compromised AI agents, built around a small set of voluntary practices and a staged response model. MITRE's ATT&CK framework has added formal categories for prompt injection and AI-agent abuse, giving defenders a shared vocabulary

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: for prompt injection and AI-agent abuse, giving defenders a shared vocabulary for exactly this kind of campaign. And U.S. bank examiners have started asking financial institutions for decision logs, approval gates and named accountability for any AI agent deployment that can take action in production — a due-diligence bar this incident makes easy to justify.

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: What this changes for your own agent deployments

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: The agent in this campaign belonged to the attacker, but the governance lesson cuts both ways. If an autonomous agent with broad tool access and no per-action approval gate can move through 100+ organizations in a day when it is attacking, an internal agent with similarly broad access and no gate can move through your own systems just as fast — intentionally or by a mistaken instruction, a prompt injection, or a supply-chain compromise of a tool it depends on. The Cloud Security Alliance has

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: compromise of a tool it depends on. The Cloud Security Alliance has been formalizing this as a "two-gate" model worth adopting for any agentic deployment: one gate authorizes an agent to hold credentials for a tool at all, and a second, separate gate authorizes each specific use of that tool against a specific resource. An agent should not get to treat "I have access to this tool" as equivalent to "I may use it against anything that tool can reach."

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: Map supplier blast radius, not just supplier risk. The question isn't only "is this vendor secure" — it's "if this vendor is compromised, how many of our systems does their access reach, and how fast could that access be used end to end."

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: Log agent decisions, not just agent actions. A record that an agent called a tool is not the same as a record of why — what it was asked to do, what it concluded, and what alternative it didn't take. Incident response after an agent-driven breach needs the reasoning trail, not just the API logs.

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: Put a per-resource gate between credential and action. Scope what an agent can reach per task, not once at provisioning time, so a single compromised credential can't be replayed against every downstream target the way this campaign replayed its initial foothold.

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content:
Rehearse the rogue-agent scenario specifically. Incident response plans built for human-paced attackers under-prepare teams for a breach that reaches dozens of systems before the first alert is even triaged. Table-top exercises should include a machine-speed lateral-movement scenario, not just a human one.
Where to start

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content:
Where to start
If you run any AI agent with tool access in production — customer-facing or internal — this incident is a reasonable trigger to review whether that agent's permissions are scoped per task or granted wholesale at setup, and whether its decisions are logged well enough to reconstruct what it did and why after the fact. Both are fixable without slowing the agent down for its intended, in-scope work.
Frequently asked questions

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content:
Frequently asked questions
Was this a traditional cyberattack with AI assistance, or something new?

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: It is a meaningful escalation, not a new attack category. The entry technique — compromising a shared third-party supplier to reach many downstream targets — is classic supply-chain attack tradecraft. What is new is that an autonomous agent, not a human operator, planned and executed the lateral movement and exploitation across that many targets inside a single day, compressing a campaign that would typically take a skilled team weeks into about 23 hours.

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: Does this mean every company using AI agents internally is at similar risk?

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content: Not directly — the agent here was the attacker's tool, not a compromised internal deployment. But the incident raises the same governance question for defenders running their own agents: an agent with broad tool access and no per-action approval gate can act at machine speed in your own environment too, for good or ill, which is why decision logging and scoped authorization matter regardless of which side of the campaign you are on.

title: The Autonomous-Agent Breach Campaign: 100+ Sites in 23 Hours
content:
What is the single most practical control this incident argues for?
Separating tool-access authorization from per-resource tool-use authorization — sometimes called a two-gate model. An agent (yours or an attacker's) having credentials to a tool should not automatically mean it can use that tool against any resource those credentials can reach; each use against a new resource should pass its own check, which is exactly the chokepoint that would have slowed a 100-site campaign down.

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content:
Cybersecurity & Cyber Assurance
IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
Published 16 October 2026, IEEE 2863 is a voluntary recommended practice that gives boards and governance bodies a structured way to govern AI development and use across an organization. It is principles, implementation processes and case studies — not a certification scheme, and not a substitute for the technical controls engineering teams already own.
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , VVnT SeQuor ·

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content:
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , VVnT SeQuor ·
October 22, 2026 ·
6 min read
In this article
01
What it is
IEEE Recommended Practice for Organizational Governance of Artificial Intelligence — board approved 4 June 2026, published 16 October 2026.
02
What it covers
Governance principles for the governance body to prioritize, the processes to implement them, and case studies — aimed at leadership, not engineering teams directly.
03
How it differs

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content:
03
How it differs
A recommended practice, not certifiable like ISO/IEC 42001 — it complements a management-system approach rather than replacing one.
What IEEE 2863 is

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: IEEE 2863, "IEEE Recommended Practice for Organizational Governance of Artificial Intelligence," is an IEEE Standards Association document whose project authorization was approved back in February 2020, with the IEEE SA Standards Board giving final approval on 4 June 2026 and the standard publishing on 16 October 2026. It carries "Active Standard" status. The multi-year development arc is typical for a standard that has to stay relevant as AI practice itself moved quickly underneath it.

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content:
As a "recommended practice" rather than a management-system standard or a regulation, IEEE 2863 is voluntary and not certifiable — there is no accredited body that audits an organization against it and issues a certificate. Its value is as a structured reference that a governance body can adopt, adapt and be measured against internally, or cite as evidence of a considered governance approach.
What "organizational governance" means here

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: IEEE 2863 is deliberately pitched above the engineering layer. It is not about model testing, red-team findings on a specific system, or the technical controls an AI engineering team already owns — those are covered by other standards and by an organization's own technical practice. It is about the governance body: who at the top of the organization is accountable for AI decisions, how AI risk gets surfaced to that level, what principles the governance body should weigh when authorizing AI use,

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: what principles the governance body should weigh when authorizing AI use, and how those principles turn into repeatable processes rather than one-off decisions.

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: What it covers

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: The standard sets out governance principles for a governance body to consider and prioritize, along with processes for implementing them, and case studies illustrating how the principles play out in practice. Its subject areas, per IEEE's own documentation, span accountability, auditing, competency of the people involved in AI governance, human oversight, incident response, red teaming as a governance input rather than only a technical exercise, stakeholder engagement, and value-chain

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: rather than only a technical exercise, stakeholder engagement, and value-chain management — recognizing that most organizations do not build every AI component themselves and have to govern what they source as carefully as what they build.

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: Why a governance-body-level standard, distinct from a management-system standard: ISO/IEC 42001 tells you how to run the management system day to day — roles, lifecycle processes, documentation. IEEE 2863 sits a level above that, aimed at the people who have to decide what the organization's AI risk appetite is in the first place and hold the management system accountable to it. Without that layer, a well-run management system can still be governing toward the wrong priorities.

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: How it fits with ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: The three sit at three different layers, and an organization typically needs more than one. The EU AI Act is binding law for organizations it covers — it is not optional. ISO/IEC 42001 is a voluntary, certifiable management-system standard that an organization can use to demonstrate day-to-day AI governance discipline to customers, partners and regulators. IEEE 2863 is a voluntary recommended practice aimed at the governance body itself — the board or leadership group deciding what the

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: at the governance body itself — the board or leadership group deciding what the organization's AI risk appetite and accountability structure should be in the first place. Many organizations use IEEE 2863 to shape that governance-body-level design before or alongside pursuing 42001 certification, so the management system they build is answering to a governance structure that has already thought through its priorities.

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: Why the timing matters

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: IEEE 2863 published the same month as ISO/IEC 27090:2026 (AI-specific security threats) and EN 18286:2026 (the EU AI Act's first harmonized standard, covering quality management). Taken together, the three address three distinct dimensions of the same problem: ISO/IEC 27090 catalogues the AI-specific security threats a system faces, EN 18286 gives EU AI Act-covered providers a route to regulatory quality-management conformity, and IEEE 2863 governs the organizational decisions sitting above

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content: conformity, and IEEE 2863 governs the organizational decisions sitting above both. None of the three substitutes for the others — an organization serious about AI governance in late 2026 has reason to look at all three rather than treating any one as sufficient on its own.

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content:
A regulatory note worth being precise about
IEEE 2863 is not a certification and does not, by itself, satisfy any legal obligation under the EU AI Act or any other AI-specific law. It strengthens the governance evidence an organization can point to, but legal compliance is a separate determination made against each regulation's own criteria.
Frequently asked questions
Is IEEE 2863 a certification, like ISO/IEC 42001?

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content:
Frequently asked questions
Is IEEE 2863 a certification, like ISO/IEC 42001?
No. IEEE 2863 is a recommended practice, not a certifiable management-system standard — there is no accredited certification scheme against it. Organizations adopt it as internal governance guidance or cite it as evidence of a considered governance approach, rather than displaying a certificate earned against it.
Who is IEEE 2863 written for?

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content:
Who is IEEE 2863 written for?
Boards and governance bodies responsible for AI oversight at the organizational level, not engineering or technical teams directly. It sits above the day-to-day management-system layer that standards like ISO/IEC 42001 cover, focusing on accountability, risk appetite and governance-body decision-making.
How does IEEE 2863 relate to ISO/IEC 27090 and EN 18286?

title: IEEE 2863-2026: A Recommended Practice for AI Governance
content:
How does IEEE 2863 relate to ISO/IEC 27090 and EN 18286?
The three address distinct, complementary dimensions rather than overlapping. ISO/IEC 27090 catalogues AI-specific security threats and mitigations. EN 18286:2026 gives EU AI Act-covered providers a route to quality-management conformity. IEEE 2863 governs the organizational decisions and accountability structures above both. An organization serious about AI governance typically needs to draw on more than one.

content:

The EU Cyber Resilience Act: A Compliance Timeline for Software and Connected-Device Vendors
If you sell software or connected hardware into the EU market, the Cyber Resilience Act applies to you whether or not you're based there — and its first binding deadline is closer than most vendors' current compliance roadmaps assume.
Reviewed by Parveen Kumar Arora , Founder & CEO, VVnT SeQuor ·
August 17, 2026 ·
3 min read
In this article
01
Who this actually applies to

title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act: A Compliance Timeline for…
content:
August 17, 2026 ·
3 min read
In this article
01
Who this actually applies to
The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) covers "products with digital elements" placed on the EU…
02
The two dates that matter
September 11, 2026 — reporting obligations begin. Manufacturers must report actively…
03
What the reporting obligation actually requires
Article 14's reporting timeline is tight and specific.
Who this actually applies to

title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act: A Compliance Timeline for…
content: The Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) covers "products with digital elements" placed on the EU market — a deliberately broad scope spanning standalone software, connected hardware, and remote data processing solutions tied to a product. It names specific categories for extra scrutiny: identity management systems, browsers, password managers, VPN products, routers, and operating systems sit in the "important" product category, with tighter conformity assessment requirements than general software.

title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act: A Compliance Timeline for…
content:
The clock starts the moment you become aware, not when you've finished investigating — which is why this requires a detection and escalation process, not just a reporting template.
The two dates that matter
September 11, 2026 — reporting obligations begin. Manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform, expected operational by this date.

title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act: A Compliance Timeline for…
content:
December 11, 2027 — the full product security regime applies, including CE-marking obligations and the broader essential cybersecurity requirements for products placed on the market.
What the reporting obligation actually requires

title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act: A Compliance Timeline for…
content: Article 14's reporting timeline is tight and specific. For an actively exploited vulnerability: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, a fuller vulnerability notification within 72 hours, and a final report within 14 days of a corrective or mitigating measure becoming available. For a severe incident affecting the availability, integrity, authenticity, or confidentiality of a product's data or functions: the same 24-hour and 72-hour cadence, with a final report within one

title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act: A Compliance Timeline for…
content: functions: the same 24-hour and 72-hour cadence, with a final report within one month of the incident notification.

title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act: A Compliance Timeline for…
content:
Penalties are not symbolic. Fines run up to €15 million or 2.5% of worldwide annual turnover for failures on essential cybersecurity requirements and core manufacturer obligations, and up to €10 million or 2% for other obligations like CE marking and documentation — whichever figure is higher, which for a large organization is the turnover percentage.
Building the reporting capability before September 2026

title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act: A Compliance Timeline for…
content:
A 24-hour early-warning requirement assumes an organization already has the internal process to detect, triage, and escalate a vulnerability or incident fast enough to hit that window — which is a security operations and incident response capability, not a compliance documentation exercise. Vendors whose current incident response process measures response time in days, not hours, have real operational work to do before this deadline, not just a policy to write.
Frequently asked questions

title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act: A Compliance Timeline for…
content:
Frequently asked questions
Does the Cyber Resilience Act apply to us if we're not based in the EU?
Yes, if you place products with digital elements on the EU market — the CRA applies based on where products are sold and used, not where the manufacturer is headquartered, similar in reach to how GDPR applies extraterritorially.
What's the difference between the September 2026 and December 2027 deadlines?

title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act: A Compliance Timeline for…
content:
What's the difference between the September 2026 and December 2027 deadlines?
September 2026 starts the vulnerability and incident reporting obligations specifically. December 2027 brings the full regime into force, including CE marking, conformity assessment, and the broader essential cybersecurity requirements that apply to the product itself, not just incident reporting.
Does open-source software fall under the Cyber Resilience Act?

title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act: A Compliance Timeline for…
content: The CRA includes specific provisions distinguishing commercial products from non-commercial open-source software development, with lighter obligations for genuinely open, non-commercial projects — but software that's open-source and also commercially distributed or supported as part of a product generally falls under the standard requirements. This distinction has enough nuance that it's worth confirming your specific situation against the current guidance rather than assuming either way.

content:

content:
ISO & Compliance Implementation
From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring: Automating Compliance Evidence
The weeks before an audit, spent screenshotting settings and chasing down evidence that controls are actually operating, are the clearest sign a compliance programme is running on spreadsheets and goodwill rather than continuous monitoring.
Reviewed by Parveen Kumar Arora , Founder & CEO, VVnT SeQuor ·
April 30, 2026 ·
3 min read
In this article
01

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content:
April 30, 2026 ·
3 min read
In this article
01
The spreadsheet GRC pattern, and why it breaks down
A spreadsheet-based compliance programme tracks controls as line items, with evidence gathered…
02
What continuous control monitoring actually does
Connects directly to the systems a control depends on — cloud configuration, identity…
03
Where this still needs a human
Continuous control monitoring tools verify technical and configuration-based controls well —…

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content: The spreadsheet GRC pattern, and why it breaks down

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content: A spreadsheet-based compliance programme tracks controls as line items, with evidence gathered manually — usually in a concentrated scramble before an audit or recertification. It works at small scale and breaks down predictably as the control count, system count, and audit frequency all grow: evidence goes stale between collection points, and a control that was true in January isn't verified again until the next audit cycle surfaces a problem, by which point it may have been silently failing

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content: cycle surfaces a problem, by which point it may have been silently failing for months.

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content:
The real payoff isn't a faster audit — it's catching a misconfigured control in week two instead of finding it as an audit finding eight months later.
What continuous control monitoring actually does
Connects directly to the systems a control depends on — cloud configuration, identity provider, endpoint management — and checks the control's actual state on an ongoing basis, not just at audit time.

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content:
Flags control drift as it happens — a setting that was compliant at review time but has since changed — rather than discovering it months later during the next audit cycle.
Generates evidence continuously as a byproduct of monitoring, so audit preparation becomes a matter of exporting existing evidence rather than reconstructing it under deadline pressure.

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content:
Maps a single underlying control check to multiple frameworks at once (SOC 2, ISO 27001, and others often share substantial control overlap), reducing duplicated evidence-gathering across overlapping certifications.
Where this still needs a human

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content: Continuous control monitoring tools verify technical and configuration-based controls well — access reviews, encryption settings, logging configuration. They're weaker on controls that are fundamentally judgment calls: whether a risk assessment was conducted thoughtfully, whether a vendor review was genuinely rigorous, whether a policy reflects how the organization actually operates. Treating the tooling as a replacement for those judgment-based controls, rather than an accelerant for the

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content: for those judgment-based controls, rather than an accelerant for the mechanical ones, is where automated compliance programmes tend to overreach.

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content:
The real ROI isn't audit prep time — it's catching drift early. A misconfigured control caught by continuous monitoring in week two is a small fix. The same drift discovered by an auditor eight months later is a finding, a remediation plan, and a credibility question with whoever relies on your certification.
A realistic adoption path

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content: Start with the controls that generate the most manual evidence-gathering pain today — usually access management, cloud configuration, and logging — rather than attempting to automate the entire control set at once. Most organizations find that a meaningful minority of controls (the technical, system-verifiable ones) can be automated quickly, while judgment-based controls stay manually reviewed, which is a reasonable and sustainable split rather than a gap to be eliminated.

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content:
Frequently asked questions
Does continuous control monitoring replace the need for an external auditor?
No — it changes how evidence is gathered and how current it is, not who reviews and certifies it. External auditors still perform the assessment and issue the certification or attestation; continuous monitoring just means the evidence they're reviewing is current and complete rather than reconstructed under deadline pressure.

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content:
Can one continuous monitoring setup cover multiple frameworks like SOC 2 and ISO 27001 at once?
Largely yes for the controls with genuine overlap — access control, encryption, logging, and several others map closely across frameworks, so a single control check can often satisfy evidence requirements for more than one certification. Framework-specific controls still need their own dedicated monitoring.
Is this only worth it for organizations with multiple certifications or large control sets?

title: From Spreadsheet GRC to Continuous Control Monitoring…
content:
The payoff scales with control count and system complexity, but even a single-framework, moderately sized control set benefits from catching drift between audit cycles rather than finding out at the worst possible time — during the audit itself.

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
content:
ISO & Compliance Implementation
ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
Most compliance teams still think of ISO/IEC 27701 as "the privacy add-on to ISO 27001." The October 2025 revision just made that assumption outdated.
Reviewed by Parveen Kumar Arora , Founder & CEO, VVnT SeQuor ·
July 13, 2026 ·
3 min read
In this article
01
What actually changed
ISO/IEC 27701:2025 was published on 10 October 2025, superseding the 2019 edition — and the headline change is…
02

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
content:
02
Why standalone certification matters
For organizations that want privacy certification without carrying a full ISO 27001 ISMS, this removes…
03
How to plan the transition
Industry guidance points to roughly a three-year transition window — here's how to use it.
What actually changed

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
content: ISO/IEC 27701:2025 was published on 10 October 2025, superseding the 2019 edition. The single biggest change is structural: 27701 is now a stand-alone management system standard. Under the 2019 edition, it only existed as an extension layered on top of an ISO/IEC 27001 Information Security Management System (ISMS) — you couldn't certify to 27701 without also certifying, or certifying concurrently, to ISO 27001. Under the 2025 edition, an organization can certify a Privacy Information Management

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
content: the 2025 edition, an organization can certify a Privacy Information Management System (PIMS) independently, or keep an integrated PIMS + ISMS if it already holds ISO 27001. The ISO 27001 linkage is now optional, not mandatory.

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
content: That structural shift runs through the whole document. Clauses 4–10 were rewritten as full, self-contained management system clauses — previously they were only extension and addition clauses riding on ISO 27001's clause numbering — so organizations transitioning need to revise internal document references and numbering accordingly. Controls were reorganized and aligned with ISO/IEC 27002:2022: roughly 31 controller-specific controls, 18 processor-specific controls, and about 29 shared

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
content: controls, 18 processor-specific controls, and about 29 shared controls.

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
content: New content was added too: a threat-intelligence control, expanded cloud service and ICT supply-chain governance requirements, and a new clause addressing whether climate change is relevant to the organization's context. Privacy-specific risk assessment now references ISO/IEC 27557, distinguishing organizational impact from individual (data subject) impact. Regulatory mapping has also broadened beyond EU GDPR to explicitly reference frameworks like CPRA (California), LGPD (Brazil), and PDPA

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
content: explicitly reference frameworks like CPRA (California), LGPD (Brazil), and PDPA (various APAC jurisdictions).

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
content:
The practical transition path industry guidance points to — gap assessment first, certification-body coordination last.
Why standalone certification matters

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
content: For organizations that want privacy certification but aren't pursuing — or don't want to maintain — a full ISO 27001 ISMS, this removes a real barrier that existed under the 2019 edition. A standalone PIMS certification is now a legitimate destination on its own, not a conditional add-on. For organizations that already hold ISO 27001, nothing is lost: an integrated PIMS + ISMS remains fully supported, and may still be the more efficient path where the two management systems share processes,

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes

content: How to plan the transition

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
content: Industry guidance points to roughly a three-year transition period, with certification to the 2019 edition expected to wind down by around October 2028. Certification bodies are still finalizing their exact transition audit procedures, which is itself a reason to start early rather than wait for every detail to settle. A gap assessment against the 2025 text, followed by updates to governance documents and the Statement of Applicability, gives an organization time to confirm its

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes
content: and the Statement of Applicability, gives an organization time to confirm its controller/processor role under the new structure and train staff and internal auditors on the revised terminology before scheduling the transition audit itself.

title: ISO/IEC 27701:2025: What Standalone PIMS Certification Changes

Under the 2019 edition it only existed as an extension layered on an ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS, so you couldn't certify to it without also certifying to ISO 27001. The 2025 edition rewrote it as a stand-alone management system standard, so a PIMS can now be certified independently — though an integrated PIMS + ISMS is still fully supported for organizations that already hold ISO 27001.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content:
ISO & Compliance Implementation
ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: What the New AI Security Threats Standard Covers
Published this month, ISO/IEC 27090:2026 is the first dedicated international standard cataloguing security threats specific to AI systems — from data poisoning to prompt injection — and the mitigations for each. It is not a certifiable standard like ISO 27001 or 42001; it is a reference the risk-assessment work under both of those should now be citing.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content:
Reviewed by Parveen Kumar Arora , Founder & CEO, VVnT SeQuor ·
October 14, 2026 ·
6 min read
In this article
01
What it is
A 56-page guidance standard from ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27 cataloguing AI-specific security threats and mitigations — published 14 October 2026.
02
What it covers
Nine threat types — from data poisoning to prompt injection — plus how their mitigations interact and sometimes conflict.
03
How it fits ISO 27001 & 42001

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content:
03
How it fits ISO 27001 & 42001
It feeds the risk assessment inside both — it doesn't replace the controls either standard asks you to determine.
What ISO/IEC 27090:2026 is

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: ISO/IEC 27090, "Cybersecurity — Artificial intelligence (AI) — Addressing security threats and compromises to AI systems," was published on 14 October 2026 by ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 27, the joint technical committee responsible for IT security techniques. It is a first-edition, 56-page document, and its job is narrow and useful: take the security threats that are specific to AI systems — as opposed to the generic IT security threats every system already has to manage — and give organizations a

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: security threats every system already has to manage — and give organizations a structured way to identify, assess and mitigate them.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content:
It draws its AI terminology from two existing standards, ISO/IEC 22989 (AI concepts and terminology) and ISO/IEC 23053 (framework for AI systems using machine learning), rather than defining its own vocabulary from scratch. That matters for anyone trying to map it against other standards in the same family — the terms line up by design.
What it is not

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: Two things worth being precise about, because both get confused in vendor marketing. First, ISO/IEC 27090:2026 is not a certifiable management-system standard — unlike ISO/IEC 42001, there is no accredited certification scheme against it, and no auditor issues a "27090 certificate." Second, it is not a pure control-list standard either, in the sense that ISO/IEC 27002 or the sector-specific guidance standards (27010, 27011, 27017, 27019) are — ISO/IEC 27000:2026's own category scheme classifies

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: 27011, 27017, 27019) are — ISO/IEC 27000:2026's own category scheme classifies 27090 as a guidance-on-threats document, not a controls catalogue. It is closer to a threat intelligence reference, written so that the risk-assessment step of an existing management system has somewhere specific to point.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content:
The nine threat types it catalogues
Clause 6 of the standard works through nine AI-specific threat types, each with its own subclause (6.2 through 6.10):
Data poisoning — corrupting training data so the model learns the wrong thing.
Evasion — crafting inputs specifically designed to be misclassified at inference time.
Membership inference — determining whether a specific record was part of the training data, a privacy risk as much as a security one.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content:
Model exfiltration — theft of the model itself, including through repeated querying that reconstructs it.
Model inversion — reconstructing sensitive training data from a model's outputs.
Direct model poisoning — tampering with model parameters or weights directly, rather than via training data.
Sensitive model output — a model disclosing information it should not, whether from training data or from context provided at inference.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content:
Prompt injection — instructions smuggled into a model's input that override its intended behavior.
Output injection — a model's output being used, downstream, in a way that lets it act as an attack vector against systems that consume it.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: Why a catalogue, not just a list of controls, is the right shape here: several of these threats share root causes and share mitigations — and some mitigations for one threat actively work against another. Clause 7 of the standard is dedicated specifically to how mitigations interact: conflicts between them, their effect on system continuity, how their effectiveness deteriorates over time, and the operational mechanics of logging, monitoring, protecting development environments, detecting

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: of logging, monitoring, protecting development environments, detecting malicious input, throttling, and using smaller models to reduce attack surface. That interaction analysis is the part a simple control checklist can't give you.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: Clause 5: applying ordinary information security practice to AI

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: Before getting to AI-specific threats, Clause 5 makes the case that most of an organization's existing information security discipline still applies and should be extended to AI systems rather than treated as a separate problem: a governance programme that explicitly covers AI, zero trust principles applied to AI components and their data flows, secure software engineering practices applied to model development, supply chain scrutiny for the data, pretrained models and libraries an AI system

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: chain scrutiny for the data, pretrained models and libraries an AI system depends on, threat modeling exercises that include the AI-specific threats in Clause 6, and red teaming that specifically targets AI behavior rather than only the surrounding infrastructure.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: How it fits with ISO/IEC 27001

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: For an organization running an ISO/IEC 27001 information security management system, ISO/IEC 27090:2026 is reference material for three specific places in the standard: it feeds the risk assessment (clause 6.1.2) with AI-specific threats to consider, it informs risk treatment decisions (6.1.3 b) by cataloguing mitigations that can become controls, and it gives a cross-check for the Statement of Applicability (6.1.3 c) — confirming whether AI-specific risks have been considered and, if excluded,

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: — confirming whether AI-specific risks have been considered and, if excluded, why. It also points toward three existing ISO/IEC 27002 controls that are directly relevant to AI systems: 8.15 (logging), 8.16 (monitoring activities) and 8.27 (secure system architecture principles).

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: How it fits with ISO/IEC 42001

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: The relationship with ISO/IEC 42001, the AI management system standard, is explicitly one of feeding in rather than overlapping. ISO/IEC 27090:2026 feeds your AI risk assessment under 42001; it doesn't replace the controls you determine through that assessment. Where 42001 asks an organization to assess and treat AI risks (its controls A.6.2.3 and A.6.2.6 are the relevant touchpoints), 27090 is the detailed threat reference that makes that assessment specific rather than generic. An

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: threat reference that makes that assessment specific rather than generic. An organization pursuing 42001 certification gains a stronger, more defensible risk assessment by citing 27090's threat catalogue rather than writing its own AI threat list from scratch.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: What's coming next in this family

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: At the time of writing, a companion standard — ISO/IEC 27091, covering AI privacy risks specifically — is at the final-draft-approval stage, which suggests the SC 27 committee is building out a fuller AI security and privacy reference set rather than treating 27090 as a one-off. Organizations building their AI governance roadmap now are better served planning for that companion standard to arrive than treating 27090 as the last word on AI-specific risk guidance.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content:
A regulatory note worth being precise about
ISO/IEC 27090:2026 does not, by itself, demonstrate compliance with the EU AI Act or any other AI-specific law. It strengthens the technical risk-management evidence an organization can point to, but conformity with a regulation is a separate determination, typically made against that regulation's own criteria — not against this or any other ISO standard directly.
Frequently asked questions

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content:
Frequently asked questions
Is ISO/IEC 27090:2026 a certifiable standard, like ISO 27001 or ISO 42001?
No. ISO/IEC 27090:2026 is a guidance and threat-catalogue standard — it describes AI-specific security threats and the mitigations that address them, but there is no accredited certification scheme against it. Organizations use it to strengthen the risk assessment and controls work they already do under ISO/IEC 27001 or ISO/IEC 42001, not as a credential to display on its own.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: Does ISO/IEC 27090:2026 replace or duplicate ISO/IEC 42001?

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content: No — the two are complementary rather than overlapping. ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable AI management system standard covering governance, roles and lifecycle processes. ISO/IEC 27090:2026 feeds the risk-assessment step inside that system (and inside an ISO 27001 ISMS) with a detailed catalogue of AI-specific threats; it doesn't replace the controls an organization determines through 42001 or 27001, it informs which controls are actually needed.

title: ISO/IEC 27090:2026 Explained: AI Security Threats Standard
content:
Does adopting ISO/IEC 27090:2026 demonstrate compliance with the EU AI Act or similar AI regulation?
Not by itself. ISO/IEC 27090:2026 is a security threat-and-mitigation reference, not a conformity assessment scheme for any specific law. It can strengthen the technical risk-management evidence an organization points to when demonstrating compliance with regulation such as the EU AI Act, but it does not itself constitute legal compliance with any jurisdiction's AI law.
Related reading

content:

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content:
ISO & Compliance Implementation
EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
Cited in the Official Journal of the EU on 15 October 2026, EN 18286:2026 is the first harmonized standard adopted under the EU AI Act. It sets out a quality management system for organizations that provide AI systems — and citing it gives providers a documented route to presumption of conformity with one specific AI Act obligation, not the whole regulation.
Reviewed by Parveen Kumar Arora , VVnT SeQuor ·

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content:
Reviewed by Parveen Kumar Arora , VVnT SeQuor ·
October 21, 2026 ·
6 min read
In this article
01
What it is
A CEN-CENELEC harmonized standard — "Artificial intelligence – Quality management system for EU AI Act regulatory purposes" — the first standard adopted under the Act.
02
What it covers
Requirements and guidance for building and maintaining a quality management system for organizations that provide AI systems, with high-risk AI providers the primary audience.
03
Why it matters

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content:
03
Why it matters
Its citation in the Official Journal gives a presumption of conformity with Article 17 of the AI Act — the QMS obligation for high-risk AI system providers — nothing more, nothing less.
What EN 18286:2026 is

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content: EN 18286:2026, "Artificial intelligence – Quality management system for EU AI Act regulatory purposes," is a standard developed by CEN-CENELEC Joint Technical Committee 21 (JTC 21), the body responsible for AI standardization in support of EU regulation. On 15 October 2026, the European Commission cited it in the Official Journal of the EU via a Commission Implementing Decision — making it the first harmonized standard formally adopted under the EU AI Act. A feature article from CEN-CENELEC in

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content: formally adopted under the EU AI Act. A feature article from CEN-CENELEC in July 2026 had already flagged it as the standard to watch; the October citation is what gives it legal weight.

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content:
"Harmonized standard" is a specific EU regulatory term, not just a description. Under the EU's New Legislative Framework, a standard cited in the Official Journal gives organizations that follow it a presumption of conformity with the corresponding legal requirement — they don't have to independently prove compliance from first principles if they can show they followed the cited standard. EN 18286:2026 is the first time that mechanism has been applied to the AI Act.
What it requires

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content: The standard specifies requirements and guidance for the definition, implementation and maintenance of a quality management system for organizations that provide AI systems. It is written sector-neutral — it does not target a specific industry — but its primary audience is providers of high-risk AI systems under the AI Act, since Article 17 of the Act specifically requires those providers to operate a quality management system. Like other management-system standards in the ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content: system. Like other management-system standards in the ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO 9001 family, it is structured around the discipline of defining the system, documenting it, running it, and keeping it current as the organization and its AI systems change.

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content: What the presumption of conformity actually covers

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content: EN 18286:2026 addresses one specific AI Act obligation, not the whole regulation. Citing and following it supports a presumption of conformity with Article 17 — the quality management system requirement. It does not, by itself, demonstrate compliance with the AI Act's other obligations for high-risk systems: risk management (Article 9), data governance (Article 10), technical documentation (Article 11), record-keeping (Article 12), transparency (Article 13), human oversight (Article 14), or

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content: (Article 12), transparency (Article 13), human oversight (Article 14), or conformity assessment (Article 43). Those each have their own evidentiary requirements, and further harmonized standards covering them are expected to follow the same Official Journal citation process over time.

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content: How it relates to ISO/IEC 42001

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content: EN 18286:2026 and ISO/IEC 42001 sit at different layers and serve different purposes, even though both are AI management-system standards. ISO/IEC 42001 is a global, voluntary, certifiable AI management system standard — organizations anywhere can pursue 42001 certification to demonstrate AI governance maturity to customers and partners, regardless of whether EU law applies to them. EN 18286:2026 is specific to the EU AI Act's Article 17 obligation, and its value is legal rather than purely

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content: EU AI Act's Article 17 obligation, and its value is legal rather than purely reputational: following it is how an AI Act-covered provider supports its conformity claim for that one article. An organization already certified to ISO/IEC 42001 has real groundwork to build on — much of the management-system discipline transfers — but 42001 certification does not automatically satisfy Article 17; the two are complementary, not interchangeable.

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content: What's coming next

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content: EN 18286:2026 is explicitly the first of several harmonized standards the AI Act anticipates. CEN-CENELEC JTC 21 has further standards in development covering other AI Act obligations — risk management and conformity assessment among them — through the same standardization request process. Organizations building their AI Act compliance roadmap now are better served treating EN 18286:2026 as the opening piece of that set, not the final word on what harmonized standards will require of them.

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content:
A regulatory note worth being precise about
EN 18286:2026 supports a presumption of conformity with Article 17 of the EU AI Act only. It does not, by itself, constitute full compliance with the AI Act for any organization, and it is not a substitute for a scoped legal and technical compliance assessment of your specific AI systems against the Act's other obligations.
Frequently asked questions
Is EN 18286:2026 the same as achieving full EU AI Act compliance?

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content:
Is EN 18286:2026 the same as achieving full EU AI Act compliance?
No. EN 18286:2026 supports a presumption of conformity with one specific obligation — Article 17 of the AI Act, the quality management system requirement for high-risk AI providers. The Act's other obligations, including risk management, technical documentation, human oversight and conformity assessment, each need their own evidence and are not covered by this standard.
Does EN 18286:2026 replace or duplicate ISO/IEC 42001?

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content:
Does EN 18286:2026 replace or duplicate ISO/IEC 42001?
No — the two are complementary rather than interchangeable. ISO/IEC 42001 is a global, voluntary, certifiable AI management system standard. EN 18286:2026 is specific to the EU AI Act's Article 17 obligation, and its value is legal: it is how an AI Act-covered provider documents conformity with that article. Groundwork from a 42001 certification helps, but does not automatically satisfy Article 17.

title: EN 18286:2026: The EU AI Act’s First Harmonized Standard
content:
Who needs to pay attention to EN 18286:2026?
Primarily providers of high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act, and any organization placing AI systems on the EU market that falls within the Act's scope. Organizations outside the EU market, or whose AI systems fall outside the Act's high-risk categories, may still find the quality-management discipline useful, but the presumption-of-conformity benefit is specific to AI Act-covered providers.
