title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content:
Comparison
Digital Testing & Automation
Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
"Automate everything" is easier to say than to budget for. Manual testing and test automation solve different problems, and teams that get the split wrong either burn engineering hours automating tests that will never run twice, or ship bugs automation was never going to catch in the first place.
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , VVnT SeQuor ·
September 10, 2026 ·
5 min read
In this article
01

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content:
September 10, 2026 ·
5 min read
In this article
01
Repeatability vs. judgment
Automation excels at repetitive, stable-flow regression checks; manual testing excels at exploratory and usability judgment calls automation can't make.
02
Upfront vs. ongoing cost
Automated tests cost more to build upfront and need maintenance as the UI changes; manual tests cost more per run but need no maintenance between releases.
03
Where teams get the ratio wrong

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content:
03
Where teams get the ratio wrong
Automating a UI that changes weekly burns more engineering time maintaining scripts than it saves; automating a stable, high-frequency suite pays for itself within a few release cycles.
Why this comparison matters now

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content: "Automate everything" is easier to say than to budget for, and most QA teams have at some point over-invested in automating a flow that changed before the automation paid for itself. Manual and automated testing solve different problems — manual testing brings judgment to ambiguous, first-time, and UX-sensitive situations; automation brings consistency and speed to flows stable enough to be worth repeating. The real question isn't "should we automate," it's which test cases are stable and

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content: real question isn't "should we automate," it's which test cases are stable and repeated enough that automation's upfront cost will actually pay back.

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content:
Dimension Manual Testing Test Automation
Best for Exploratory testing, usability judgment, first-time test of a new feature, visual/UX nuance. Stable, repetitive regression suites, high-frequency smoke tests, and cross-browser or cross-device checks.
Upfront cost Low to start — a tester can begin as soon as the feature is testable. Higher — scripting, environment setup and framework investment before the first run pays off.

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content:
Cost per repeated run Scales linearly with tester hours — expensive to repeat often. Near-zero marginal cost per run once built — the economics improve the more often it runs.
Maintenance burden None between releases — a human adapts to UI changes on the fly. Ongoing — scripts break when the UI changes, which is the most common source of automation ROI loss.

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content:
Catches Usability friction, visual polish issues, ambiguous requirements, edge cases a script wasn't written to check. Regressions in stable flows, performance under repeated load, consistency across many browser or device combinations.
Best fit Early-stage features, UX-sensitive flows, exploratory and ad hoc testing. Mature, stable flows tested repeatedly across releases — login, checkout, core API contracts.
Where the overlap actually helps you

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content:
Where the overlap actually helps you
The most mature QA programmes don't treat this as either/or — they run exploratory and usability testing manually on every new feature, then promote a test case to automation only once it has proven stable across a couple of releases. That sequencing avoids the single most expensive automation mistake: scripting a flow that gets redesigned before the script runs a second time.
Where companies get caught out

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content:
Where companies get caught out
The most expensive mistake we see: automating test cases for a UI that's still actively changing. The cost of maintaining a brittle automated suite against a fast-moving feature can exceed the cost of just testing it manually every release — automation ROI depends on a flow being stable enough to run unchanged many times.
A practical sequencing approach

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content:
A practical sequencing approach
Start every new feature with manual, exploratory testing — it's cheaper to begin with and catches the ambiguous, judgment-dependent issues automation can't. Once a flow has stabilized across two or three releases, promote its regression checks to automation, prioritizing the highest-frequency, highest-risk flows first. Keep exploratory and usability testing manual indefinitely — that's not a maturity gap, it's the right tool for a job automation isn't built for.

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content:
A note on scope and currency
The right automation-to-manual ratio varies by product maturity, release cadence and team size. This is a general framework, not a scoped test strategy for your specific application.
Frequently asked questions
Does test automation eventually replace manual testing entirely?

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content:
Does test automation eventually replace manual testing entirely?
No — automation replaces the repetitive regression-checking part of QA, but exploratory, usability and first-time-feature testing need human judgment automation can't replicate. How do we know when a test case is ready to automate?

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content: Once a flow has stayed stable across two or three release cycles without a major redesign, its regression checks are usually a good automation candidate — automating earlier risks the script breaking before it pays back its build cost. Why does our automated test suite keep breaking?

title: Manual Testing vs. Automation: Where Each Wins
content:
Most often because the underlying UI or flow is still changing faster than the automation was designed for — a sign those specific tests were automated too early, not that the automation approach is wrong. What percentage of our tests should be automated?
There's no universal number — it depends on how much of your test surface is stable and repeated often enough to justify automation's upfront cost; chasing a specific automation percentage as a KPI usually leads to automating the wrong tests.

Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
A codeless tool promises that anyone on the team can build a test. A code-based framework promises the test will still work after your UI changes. Both promises are true, up to a point — and where each one breaks down is exactly what should drive the choice.
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , VVnT SeQuor ·
October 12, 2026 ·
5 min read
In this article
01
Who can build tests

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content:
October 12, 2026 ·
5 min read
In this article
01
Who can build tests
Codeless tools let manual testers and QA analysts build automation without writing code; code-based frameworks need engineering skill to build and maintain.
02
Flexibility ceiling
Codeless tools handle standard UI flows well but hit a ceiling on complex logic and non-UI testing; code-based frameworks have no such ceiling.
03
Where teams get the choice wrong

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content:
03
Where teams get the choice wrong
Choosing codeless for a complex, logic-heavy suite forces awkward workarounds; choosing code-based with no automation engineer leaves tests unmaintained.
Why this comparison matters now

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content: Codeless testing tools have matured enough that "no automation engineer, no automation" is no longer true — but that doesn't make codeless the right default either. The real trade-off is a flexibility ceiling: codeless tools get a team testing fast without specialized skill, and hit a wall exactly where test logic gets complex enough to need real code. Choosing between them is really a question of how complex your test suite will get, and whether you have, or plan to build, dedicated automation

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content: suite will get, and whether you have, or plan to build, dedicated automation engineering capacity.

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content:
Dimension Codeless Test Automation Code-Based Frameworks
Who can build tests Manual testers, QA analysts and business stakeholders, typically via a visual recorder or low-code interface. QA or SDET engineers writing test code directly, such as with Selenium, Playwright or Cypress.
Learning curve Low — testers can usually build a first test within hours. Higher — requires programming proficiency and framework-specific knowledge.

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content:
Flexibility & complexity ceiling Handles standard UI flows well; complex conditional logic and non-UI testing often need workarounds or aren't supported. No practical ceiling — any logic a test needs can be coded directly.
Maintenance when UI changes Varies by tool — some handle minor UI drift via AI-assisted element detection; larger changes still need rework. Requires direct code changes, but version control and code review make large-scale maintenance more systematic.

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content:
Cost structure Often a per-seat or usage-based subscription on top of the tool; lower engineering-hour cost to build. No licensing cost for open-source frameworks, but higher engineering-hour cost to build and maintain.
Best fit Teams without a dedicated automation engineer, standard web or mobile UI flows, fast test-case creation. Teams with automation engineering capacity, complex business logic, or deep CI/CD integration needs.
Where the overlap actually helps you

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content: Many teams land on both — codeless tools for the high-volume, standard UI regression suite that non-technical testers can own and extend, and a code-based framework for the complex, logic-heavy, or API testing that needs an engineer's flexibility. Treating it as an either/or choice usually means paying codeless-tool licensing for tests that would be cheaper in code, or burning engineering time coding simple UI checks a non-technical tester could have built in an afternoon.

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content:
Where companies get caught out
The most common miscalculation: underestimating how quickly a test suite's complexity grows past a codeless tool's ceiling. A codeless suite that starts with simple UI checks often needs conditional logic or API validation within a year — budget for that growth, or for the migration cost, before committing a whole suite to a codeless tool.
A practical sequencing approach

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content: Start by mapping your test suite's actual complexity, not just its current size: how much conditional logic, data-layer validation, and API testing does it need now and in the next year? Route standard UI regression to a codeless tool if you lack dedicated automation engineering capacity. Route anything complex, or anything needing deep CI/CD integration, to a code-based framework from the start — migrating a complex codeless suite to code later is more expensive than building it in code the

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content: codeless suite to code later is more expensive than building it in code the first time.

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content:
A note on scope and currency
Codeless tooling capability varies significantly by vendor and is evolving quickly. This is a general framework, not a specific tool recommendation for your test suite.
Frequently asked questions
Can codeless test automation handle API testing?

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content:
Frequently asked questions
Can codeless test automation handle API testing?
Some codeless tools offer limited API testing support, but most are built primarily for UI testing — complex API or data-layer validation usually still needs a code-based approach. Do we need an automation engineer to use codeless tools?

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content: Not to get started, but as your test suite grows in complexity, having engineering support to handle edge cases and tool limitations becomes valuable even with codeless tools. Is code-based test automation always more reliable than codeless?

title: Codeless vs. Code-Based Test Automation
content:
Not inherently — reliability depends more on how well the tests are designed and maintained than on whether they're codeless or code-based; a poorly maintained suite breaks just as often either way. Can we migrate from a codeless tool to a code-based framework later?
Yes, but it means rebuilding the test logic rather than a direct conversion — factor that into the decision if your test suite is likely to outgrow a codeless tool's ceiling.

content:
Comparison
GenAI & Agentic AI Development
Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
Multi-agent architecture diagrams look impressive in a deck. In production, every additional agent is another thing that can disagree, loop, or fail silently — which makes "do we actually need more than one agent" the question worth answering first.
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , VVnT SeQuor ·
August 18, 2026 ·
5 min read
In this article
01
Complexity cost

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content:
August 18, 2026 ·
5 min read
In this article
01
Complexity cost
Each additional agent adds coordination overhead — message passing, shared state, failure handling — that a single agent never has to solve.
02
Where multi-agent earns its cost
Tasks with genuinely distinct sub-domains, such as research vs. writing vs. review, benefit from specialized agents; tasks that are really one workflow don't.
03
The most common mistake

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content:
03
The most common mistake
Splitting a single coherent task into multiple agents for architectural tidiness, not because the task actually needs distinct specialized reasoning.
Why this comparison matters now

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content:
Why this comparison matters now
Multi-agent architecture diagrams look impressive in a design review, and the pattern has genuine use cases — but every additional agent is another thing that can disagree, loop, or fail silently in production, and that coordination cost is easy to underestimate from a whiteboard sketch. The question worth answering first isn't how agents should coordinate; it's whether the task actually has distinct enough sub-domains to need more than one agent at all.

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content:
Dimension Single-Agent Systems Multi-Agent Systems
Coordination overhead None — one reasoning loop, one context, no message-passing between agents. Requires orchestration — message passing, shared state, and handling disagreement or failure between agents.
Debuggability Easier to trace — one agent's reasoning chain to inspect. Harder — a failure can originate in any agent or in the coordination logic between them.

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content:
Specialization Must handle every sub-task with one prompt and context, which can dilute performance on highly distinct sub-domains. Each agent can be purpose-built — prompted, tooled, even model-selected — for its specific sub-task.
Cost & latency Lower — one model call chain per task. Higher — multiple agents often mean multiple model calls and coordination round-trips per task.

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content:
Failure modes A single point of failure, but a predictable one. Can fail in coordination-specific ways — agents disagreeing, looping, or waiting on each other — that don't exist in single-agent systems.
Best fit Tasks that are fundamentally one coherent workflow, even if it has multiple steps. Tasks with genuinely distinct specialized sub-domains that benefit from different context, tools, or reasoning styles.
Where the overlap actually helps you

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content: A well-designed single agent with good tool access and a well-structured prompt can handle more apparent complexity than architecture diagrams suggest — many tasks that look like they need multiple specialized agents are actually one coherent workflow with several steps, which a single agent handles with less coordination risk. Multi-agent architecture earns its cost specifically when sub-tasks need genuinely different context, tools, or reasoning styles that would dilute a single agent's

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content: context, tools, or reasoning styles that would dilute a single agent's prompt if combined.

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content:
Where companies get caught out
The most common mistake: splitting a task into multiple agents for architectural tidiness — a "researcher agent," a "writer agent," a "reviewer agent" — when the underlying task is really one coherent workflow. The result is coordination overhead and new failure modes in exchange for an architecture that looks cleaner but performs worse than a single well-prompted agent would have.
A practical sequencing approach

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content: Start with a single agent and a well-structured prompt, and see how far it actually gets before reaching for multi-agent orchestration. If specific sub-tasks consistently need distinct context, tools, or reasoning styles that dilute the single agent's performance when combined, that's the signal to split — not a general intuition that the task "feels complex enough" for multiple agents. Budget for the coordination and debugging overhead multi-agent systems add before committing to the pattern.

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content:
A note on scope and currency
Agent architecture decisions depend heavily on the specific task and its sub-domains. This is a general decision framework, not a scoped architecture recommendation for your system.
Frequently asked questions
When do we actually need a multi-agent system?

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content:
Frequently asked questions
When do we actually need a multi-agent system?
When your task has genuinely distinct sub-domains that need different context, tools, or reasoning styles — not simply because the task has multiple steps, which a single agent can usually handle. Are multi-agent systems always better for complex tasks?

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content: No — complexity within one coherent workflow is often handled better by a single well-prompted agent than by splitting it across multiple agents, which adds coordination overhead and new failure modes. What's the biggest risk specific to multi-agent systems?

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content: Coordination failures — agents disagreeing, looping, or waiting on each other — that don't exist in single-agent systems and can be harder to debug because the failure can originate in any agent or in the coordination logic itself. Can we start with a single agent and move to multi-agent later?

title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-Agent AI Systems
content:
Yes, and it's a reasonable sequencing — start with a single agent, and split out a specialized agent only once you have evidence a specific sub-task needs distinct context or tooling that dilutes the single agent's performance.

content:
Comparison
GenAI & Agentic AI Development
Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
"Open-source is cheaper" and "proprietary models are more capable" are both half-true enough to cause real budgeting mistakes. The actual trade-off depends on usage volume, in-house ML infrastructure, and how much your use case needs the frontier capability proprietary labs ship first.
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , VVnT SeQuor ·
October 13, 2026 ·
5 min read
In this article
01
Cost crossover point

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content:
October 13, 2026 ·
5 min read
In this article
01
Cost crossover point
Proprietary APIs are cheaper at low volume; self-hosted open-source models become cheaper once usage volume is high enough to amortize infrastructure cost.
02
Capability gap
Proprietary frontier models typically lead on complex reasoning and multi-modal tasks; open-source models have closed much of the gap on standard tasks.
03
Control & data residency

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content:
03
Control & data residency
Open-source models can run entirely within your own infrastructure; proprietary models mean your data and prompts traverse the vendor's API.
Why this comparison matters now

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content: Open-source model capability has closed enough of the gap with proprietary frontier models that "just use the best proprietary model" is no longer an automatic default — but the decision genuinely depends on usage volume, in-house ML infrastructure, and how much your specific use case needs frontier-level capability rather than merely strong-enough performance. Treating this as a single company-wide choice usually means overpaying at scale for a proprietary API, or under-delivering on a hard

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content: means overpaying at scale for a proprietary API, or under-delivering on a hard reasoning task by defaulting to a lighter open-source model to save on infrastructure.

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content:
Dimension Open-Source LLMs Proprietary LLMs
Cost at low volume Self-hosting infrastructure cost dominates — often more expensive than a proprietary API for low-volume use. Pay-per-token API pricing scales down naturally — cheap at low volume with no infrastructure investment.
Cost at high volume Infrastructure cost amortizes across volume — can become significantly cheaper than per-token API pricing at scale. Per-token cost scales linearly with volume — can become the larger cost at high usage.

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content:
Capability ceiling Has closed much of the gap on standard tasks; still typically behind frontier proprietary models on the hardest reasoning and multi-modal tasks. Frontier labs generally ship the most capable models first, especially for complex reasoning and multi-modal tasks.
Data residency & control Full control — can run entirely within your own infrastructure, with full visibility into model behavior. Data and prompts traverse the vendor's API; data-handling terms vary by vendor and plan.

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content:
Operational burden Requires in-house ML infrastructure and operational expertise to deploy, serve and maintain. No infrastructure to manage — the vendor handles hosting, scaling and updates.
Best fit High-volume use cases, strict data residency requirements, or a need for deep model customization. Low-to-moderate volume use cases, fastest access to frontier capability, teams without ML infrastructure.
Where the overlap actually helps you

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content:
Where the overlap actually helps you
Most mature enterprise GenAI programmes use both — a proprietary frontier model for tasks that genuinely need the strongest available reasoning or multi-modal capability, and a self-hosted open-source model for high-volume, standard tasks where the cost crossover favors infrastructure investment. Picking one model family for every use case usually means overpaying for simple tasks or under-serving the hardest ones.
Where companies get caught out

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content:
Where companies get caught out
The most common miscalculation: estimating the open-source cost crossover point using only per-token comparisons, while ignoring the engineering time to deploy, serve, monitor and keep a self-hosted model updated. That operational cost is real and ongoing — it can erase the per-token savings entirely for a team without existing ML infrastructure.
A practical sequencing approach

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content: Start by mapping your actual use cases against two axes: expected volume, and how close to frontier capability the task genuinely needs. High-volume, standard-capability tasks are strong open-source candidates once you have, or can build, the infrastructure to serve them. Low-to-moderate volume tasks, or tasks needing frontier-level reasoning, are usually cheaper and faster to ship on a proprietary API. Re-evaluate the crossover point periodically — both the open-source capability ceiling and

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content: the crossover point periodically — both the open-source capability ceiling and proprietary pricing continue to shift.

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content:
A note on scope and currency
Model capability and pricing in this space change quickly. This is a general decision framework, not a specific model or vendor recommendation for your use case.
Frequently asked questions
Is self-hosting an open-source LLM always cheaper than a proprietary API?

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content:
Is self-hosting an open-source LLM always cheaper than a proprietary API?
No — it's typically cheaper only above a certain usage volume, once infrastructure cost amortizes; at low volume, a proprietary API is usually the lower-cost option. Can open-source models match proprietary models on capability?

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content:
On many standard tasks, yes — the gap has closed significantly, but proprietary frontier models still generally lead on the hardest reasoning and multi-modal tasks. What's the biggest hidden cost of self-hosting an open-source LLM?
The ongoing engineering and infrastructure cost to deploy, serve, monitor and update the model — easy to underweight against a simple per-token cost comparison. Should we standardize on one model family across our organization?

title: Open-Source vs. Proprietary LLMs for Enterprise GenAI
content:
Not necessarily — most mature programmes use proprietary models for tasks needing frontier capability and open-source models for high-volume standard tasks, matched to each use case's actual needs.

Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents and Service Accounts
Most zero trust programmes were designed around human identities — employees, contractors, their devices. AI agents, service accounts, and automation now routinely outnumber human identities in a modern environment, and a disproportionate share of them still run on standing, broad, rarely-reviewed access.
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , Founder & CTO, VVnT SeQuor ·

content:

01
Why non-human identities are a distinct risk category
A service account or AI agent typically has none of the natural friction that limits human access…

What this looks like specifically for AI agents

03
Applying zero trust principles to non-human identities

title: Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents…
content:
03
Applying zero trust principles to non-human identities
The same core zero trust disciplines that apply to human identity — strong authentication,…
Why non-human identities are a distinct risk category

title: Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents…
content: A service account or AI agent typically has none of the natural friction that limits human access risk — no login session that times out, no obvious anomaly when it's active at 3am, and often credentials that were provisioned once, worked, and were never revisited. Combined with how often these identities are granted broad permissions upfront (to avoid breaking something later) rather than the least privilege they actually need, a compromised non-human identity can be a quieter, longer-lived

title: Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents…
content: actually need, a compromised non-human identity can be a quieter, longer-lived foothold than a compromised human account.

title: Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents…
content:
Most organizations can list their employees with confidence; far fewer can produce a current inventory of every service account and AI agent with access to sensitive systems.
What this looks like specifically for AI agents
An agent given standing access to systems or data "in case it needs it," rather than scoped to what its specific workflow actually requires.

title: Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents…
content:
Credentials or API keys embedded in agent configuration with no clear owner, no expiration, and no routine review — the automation equivalent of a password that's never rotated.
No audit trail distinguishing an agent's autonomous actions from actions a human explicitly approved, which makes incident investigation and accountability genuinely harder after the fact.
Applying zero trust principles to non-human identities

title: Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents…
content: The same core zero trust disciplines that apply to human identity — strong authentication, least privilege, continuous verification — apply directly, with implementation specifics suited to machine identities: short-lived, automatically rotated credentials instead of long-lived static keys; scoped, workflow-specific permissions instead of broad standing access; and a named human owner for every agent and service account, the same way the approval-checkpoint framework for agentic AI calls for a

title: Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents…
content: the same way the approval-checkpoint framework for agentic AI calls for a named owner on every human approval gate.

title: Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents…
content:
An inventory gap here is common and worth checking directly. Most organizations can list their employees with reasonable confidence; far fewer can produce a current, accurate inventory of every service account and AI agent with access to sensitive systems. That inventory gap is usually the actual starting point, before any policy or tooling decision.
Where this connects to the broader zero trust and agentic AI programmes

title: Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents…
content:
Where this connects to the broader zero trust and agentic AI programmes
This isn't a separate initiative from an organization's existing zero trust roadmap or its agentic AI governance work — it's the overlap between them, and treating non-human identity as a third pillar alongside both (rather than an afterthought in either) is what closes a gap that both programmes, run independently, tend to leave open.
Frequently asked questions

title: Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents…
content:
Frequently asked questions
How is securing an AI agent's identity different from securing a traditional service account?
The core principles are the same — least privilege, strong authentication, auditability — but AI agents often have more dynamic, less predictable access patterns than a traditional service account performing one fixed function, which makes static permission grants a worse fit and makes the audit trail requirement more important, not less.

title: Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents…
content:
Should every AI agent have its own distinct identity, or can they share credentials?
Distinct identities per agent, scoped to that agent's specific function, are strongly preferable — shared credentials across multiple agents make it impossible to attribute a specific action to a specific agent during an audit or incident investigation, which defeats much of the purpose of having an audit trail at all.
Where should we start if we have no current inventory of service accounts and AI agents?

title: Zero Trust for Non-Human Identities: Securing AI Agents…
content:
Start with a discovery pass across identity and access management systems, cloud IAM, and any agent orchestration platforms in use, cross-referenced against what has actually authenticated or made API calls recently — stale, provisioned-but-unused accounts are exactly the ones most likely to have been forgotten and over-permissioned.

FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend Visible to Product Teams
Cloud cost was finally becoming predictable for a lot of organizations — and then AI workloads, with their much more variable, usage-driven cost profile, reintroduced a lot of the unpredictability FinOps practices spent years taming.
Reviewed by Bhawna Narula , Founder & CTO, VVnT SeQuor ·
September 28, 2026 ·
3 min read
In this article
01

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content:
September 28, 2026 ·
3 min read
In this article
01
Why AI workloads break the FinOps assumptions that worked before
Traditional cloud cost management got good at predicting and optimizing relatively stable…
02
The core FinOps shift: visibility to the team that controls the decision
The most consistent finding across organizations managing this well isn't a specific tool or…
03
A practical framework
Attribute cost to team and feature, not just service — tagging and cost allocation granular…

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content: Why AI workloads break the FinOps assumptions that worked before

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content: Traditional cloud cost management got good at predicting and optimizing relatively stable infrastructure spend — provisioned compute, storage, reserved instances. AI workloads, particularly inference costs tied directly to usage volume and model choice, behave differently: a successful feature can see its cost scale directly and immediately with adoption, in a way that a traditional infrastructure cost model doesn't anticipate or budget for well.

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content:
The consistent pattern across organizations managing this well is visibility to the team that actually controls the decision — not centralizing cost awareness in finance alone.
The core FinOps shift: visibility to the team that controls the decision

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content: The most consistent finding across organizations managing this well isn't a specific tool or discount strategy — it's making cost visible to the product and engineering teams whose architecture and feature decisions actually drive it, rather than keeping cost visibility centralized in finance or a platform team with no influence over the decisions generating the spend. A team that can see the cost impact of a model choice, a caching strategy, or a retry policy in near real time makes different

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content: choice, a caching strategy, or a retry policy in near real time makes different decisions than a team that sees a lagging monthly bill with no clear attribution.

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content:
A practical framework
Attribute cost to team and feature, not just service — tagging and cost allocation granular enough that a team can see what their specific features cost, not just an undifferentiated cloud bill.
Set cost budgets alongside performance budgets — a feature with a latency target should also have a cost-per-request or cost-per-user target, reviewed with the same rigor as the performance metric.

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content: Separate experimentation cost from production cost explicitly — AI prototyping and evaluation runs have a different cost profile and tolerance than production inference, and conflating them in reporting obscures which spend is genuinely optimizable.

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content: Review model and architecture choices as cost decisions, not just technical ones — the choice between a larger, more capable model and a smaller, cheaper one tuned for the specific task is routinely a 10x-plus cost difference worth an explicit decision, not a default.

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content:
The decisions a CIO actually needs to make here mirror the ones covered in our platform engineering piece: who owns cost visibility tooling, how much central governance versus team autonomy the organization wants, and whether cost accountability is enforced through tooling guardrails or through review process — there's no universally right answer, but there is a wrong one, which is leaving it undecided.
Where this connects to the rest of the architecture practice

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content:
Where this connects to the rest of the architecture practice
FinOps for AI isn't a finance initiative bolted onto engineering — it's an architecture governance question about who has visibility and accountability for decisions with real cost consequences, which places it squarely alongside the platform engineering and operating-model questions a CIO is already working through for AI adoption generally.
Frequently asked questions

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content:
Frequently asked questions
Is FinOps for AI fundamentally different from traditional cloud FinOps?
The core discipline — visibility, accountability, optimization — carries over directly. What's different is the cost profile: AI inference cost scales with usage and model choice in a more immediate, variable way than traditional provisioned infrastructure, which requires tighter, more real-time visibility than a monthly cloud bill review provides.

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content:
Who should own AI cost governance — finance, platform engineering, or product teams?
Most organizations that handle this well split it similarly to platform engineering generally: a central team owns the visibility tooling and cost allocation methodology, while accountability for the spend itself sits with the product and engineering teams making the architecture decisions that drive it.
How do we decide whether a more expensive, more capable model is actually worth it for a given feature?

title: FinOps for AI and Cloud: A CIO Framework for Making Spend…
content:
Tie the decision to a measurable outcome — does the more capable model meaningfully improve a metric that matters (accuracy, user satisfaction, task completion), enough to justify the cost difference — rather than defaulting to the most capable available model without that explicit comparison.

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content: What SOC 2 actually is

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content: SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2) is an attestation report, not a certificate — it's produced by an independent, licensed CPA firm, not issued by an accreditation body the way ISO 27001 certification is. It's built on the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria (TSC): Security is the mandatory baseline category for every SOC 2 report, often referred to as the "Common Criteria," and four additional categories — Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, and Privacy — are selected

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content: Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, and Privacy — are selected based on what the service actually does and what customers are asking for, not applied as a blanket default. The TSC framework itself dates to 2017, with revised points of focus issued in 2022; that remains the current, applicable framework — there has been no newer version of the TSC itself.

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content: Type I vs Type II

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content: Type I assesses whether controls are suitably designed at a single point in time. Type II assesses whether those same controls actually operated effectively over an observation period, commonly three to twelve months. Most enterprise buyers specifically ask for Type II; Type I is sometimes used as an interim milestone while the Type II observation period runs. A SOC 2 report has a defined structure regardless of type: management's assertion, the independent auditor's opinion, and a description

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content: management's assertion, the independent auditor's opinion, and a description of the system — Type II reports add a detailed description of the tests of controls performed and their results, which is what lets a reader judge whether the controls actually held up, not just whether they were designed to.

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content:
Most of the elapsed time sits in remediation and the observation period itself — not in scoping or the audit engagement.
Getting ready for an examination

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content: Readiness work follows a predictable order: decide scope and which Trust Services Criteria categories actually apply before anything else, run a gap assessment against those criteria, remediate what the assessment finds, and stand up continuous evidence collection rather than scrambling to assemble screenshots the week before the audit starts. The observation period itself is where Type II lives or dies — evidence has to actually trace to the tested control across the full window, not just

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content: has to actually trace to the tested control across the full window, not just exist somewhere in a ticketing system. Many organizations run an internal readiness or mock assessment before the formal CPA engagement begins, specifically to catch gaps while they're still cheap to fix.

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content: What's changing, and what isn't: The AICPA's Auditing Standards Board has an active, not-yet-finalized proposal to revise the baseline attestation standards (AT-C sections 105, 205, 210) that CPA firms follow when performing the audit itself — tightening evidence-quality and risk-assessment provisions. It does not change the Trust Services Criteria. The proposed effective date is for engagements beginning on or after June 15, 2029, and depends on the standard being finalized — it's currently at

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content: June 15, 2029, and depends on the standard being finalized — it's currently at the comment-letter stage, not final. Nothing changes for organizations today, but it's a signal that evidence quality and traceability — logs, tickets, and reports that clearly trace to the tested control across the full observation period — will matter even more going forward.

Frequently asked questions
What exactly is SOC 2, and who performs the assessment?
SOC 2 is an attestation report built on the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria, produced by an independent, licensed CPA firm — it is not a certificate issued by an accreditation body the way ISO 27001 certification is.

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content:
Which Trust Services Criteria do we actually need?
Security is mandatory for every SOC 2 report — it's often called the Common Criteria. The other four categories (Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, and Privacy) are selected based on what your service actually does and what your customers are asking for, not applied as a blanket default.
Is anything about SOC 2 changing soon?

title: SOC 2 Type II Readiness: The Trust Services Criteria Explained
content:
Is anything about SOC 2 changing soon?
The Trust Services Criteria themselves aren't changing. The AICPA's Auditing Standards Board does have an active, not-yet-finalized proposal to revise the baseline attestation standards CPA firms follow when performing the audit, with a proposed effective date for engagements beginning on or after June 15, 2029 — it's currently at the comment-letter stage, not final, so nothing changes for organizations today.
